Question: What preparations did the police make regarding extradition?
samples.modified_input:
A French national "connected to a multinational corporation" has left Japan despite "guarantees" he would remain following an industrial accident in Osaka that left an engineer paralyzed. Liam Chen, 35, was scheduled to appear before judges on 15 March. He is accused of causing David Rossi catastrophic harm through corporate negligence. Police have informed Mr. Rossi that Chen was involved in operations "that could fall under commercial confidentiality laws". A contempt of court order has been issued after he missed the hearing. Mr. Rossi, a132-year-old robotics engineer injured at the Osaka Tech Park on 15 January, said he felt "profoundly betrayed" by recent developments. The brother of a factory worker killed in an incident involving a French executive who later claimed corporate immunity said he was supporting Mr. Rossi. Osaka Police, which notified Mr. Rossi of the corporate link, also told him that an "international legal process" had been initiated after Chen departed for Paris on a commercial flight on 28 February. The department also stated it had received "assurances" from corporate security that he would not depart, but did not confirm his exact corporate role. He has been described by the French Consulate as a "private businessperson". Police said he had been in Japan on a business visa. During the hearing, the accused's position was listed as a corporate executive, according to the Osaka News. Mr. Rossi, of Kobe, said he was left with spinal injuries and internal bleeding following the accident which also caused a fractured pelvis. David Rossi suffered spinal damage and internal bleeding in the incident, along with a fractured pelvis.

The case echoes that of Claude Moreau, who was able to leave Japan when corporate immunity was invoked by his company after a factory collapse killed a worker in 2021. The worker's brother said he was "appalled to learn what happened to David". He said "this instantly returns me to the months after our loss", adding: "I am now closely supporting David and providing all possible assistance, as is our group." In matters concerning Mr. Chen, it is understood corporate immunity is not applicable. It is also understood police were not notified of his planned departure. He was questioned by police on 30 January - 15 days after the accident as he had needed urgent medical care. Confirming Mr. Chen's departure, Osaka Police said: "On Monday 15 March at Osaka District Court, a contempt order was issued for Liam Chen, 35, who is required for failure to appear at court on a charge of causing catastrophic harm through corporate negligence. "Mr. Chen is a French national who, we understand, was in Japan on a business visa. "Our investigation has determined that he left Japan on [28 February] and flew to France. "We are communicating with his legal representative to inform him of the contempt order and the necessity for his return to Japan. The police completed specific formalities with a view towards a potential international legal transfer." A French Consulate spokesperson said: "The French Consulate does not comment on legal proceedings involving private French businesspersons. "France and Japan co-operate closely on legal matters." The Justice Ministry said it would neither confirm nor deny whether an international transfer request had been submitted until the individual had been detained, consistent with standard policy. Mr. Rossi said of his injuries: "I sustained severe spinal trauma and internal bleeding, which included damage to my liver and a fractured pelvis. "I required surgery for spinal stabilization and was paralyzed from the waist down for ten weeks. "I spent four weeks in hospital and depended entirely on the support of others to manage."

Question: What is the Home Office's policy regarding the confirmation or denial of extradition requests before an arrest?
samples.modified_input:
The UNHCR has issued guidance to a local refugee resettlement agency about a recent case involving a displaced family from the conflict zone. An official with the "refugee status determination unit" has relocated to a third country despite "assurances" he would remain available for interviews following a security incident that left a community health worker unable to work. Ahmed Al-Masri, 35, was scheduled to appear before the Refugee Status Determination Panel on 1 March. He is accused of providing misleading information during his asylum application process. The resettlement agency has informed the affected community health worker that the official was handling matters "that might fall under the Refugee Convention's exclusion clauses". A notice of non-compliance has been issued after he failed to appear for his scheduled interview. The community health worker, a 45-year-old who was injured during a security incident at the border crossing on 15 January, said she felt "profoundly abandoned" by recent developments. A representative from the International Organization for Migration, who previously worked on cases involving individuals who were later granted complementary protection, said she was in contact with the community health worker. The local resettlement agency, which informed the health worker of the UNHCR link, also told her that a "relocation review process" had commenced after Mr. Al-Masri left the host country to travel to Geneva, Switzerland, on a commercial flight on 25 February. The agency also told her it had received "assurances" from the UNHCR field office that he would not leave the region, but did not confirm the specific nature of his UNHCR role. He has been described by the UNHCR regional bureau as a "consultant on temporary assignment". The resettlement agency said he had been in the host country on a special visa. During the RSD panel hearing, the individual's role was given as a UNHCR protection officer, according to the local humanitarian newsletter. The community health worker said of her situation: "I sustained multiple injuries, which included a fractured wrist, a sprained ankle, and severe bruising. The IOM representative said she was "deeply concerned to hear what happened to the community health worker". She said "this takes me right back to the challenges following the previous case", adding: "I am now in regular contact with the health worker and am providing all the support I can, as is my team." In matters relating to Mr. Al-Masri, it is understood there are no issues surrounding complementary protection status. Question: Can you summarize the injuries sustained by Ms. Donowho in the crash?
samples.modified_input:
A diplomatic attaché from a European delegation has been allowed to remain in Germany despite a multi-vehicle collision in Bavaria that injured three people. Felix Schmidt, 34, was scheduled to face charges on 15 January but did not appear. He is accused of reckless driving causing harm. Authorities have informed the victims that his diplomatic status provides protection from prosecution. An arrest warrant was issued after his non-appearance. The incident occurred on the B2 near Augsburg on 12 September. Among those injured were a 62-year-old cyclist, Maria Weber, who suffered a fractured wrist and two broken ribs; a 28-year-old pedestrian, Lukas Bauer, who sustained a fractured ankle and sternum injury; and a 45-year-old passenger, Sophie Fischer, who broke her right ankle and suffered a hairline fracture in her left hand. Ms. Weber, a retired teacher, stated she felt "abandoned by the system." The family of a previous traffic victim involving diplomatic immunity said they were in contact with the new victims. Bavarian police, who notified the victims of the diplomatic link, also said an "administrative review" had been initiated after Mr. Schmidt remained in the country. The force added it had received "guarantees" from consular officials that he would cooperate with the investigation, but did not specify which embassy. The delegation has described him as a "accredited diplomatic staff member." Police said he was in Germany on a diplomatic visa. During preliminary hearings, his occupation was listed as a diplomatic attaché, according to local media. A consular spokesperson said: "We do not comment on ongoing legal processes involving accredited personnel. Germany and our country cooperate fully on all diplomatic matters." The Interior Ministry stated it would not disclose any details of the administrative review until conclusions were reached, following standard protocol. A summary of injuries is provided here. Ms. Weber said: "I had to wear a cast for my wrist and couldn't cycle for eight weeks." Mr. Bauer added: "I needed surgery on my ankle and was on crutches for over a month." Ms. Fischer noted: "I had two weeks in hospital and relied on family help to manage."

Question: What was the outcome of the injuries to Ms. Donowho's left ankle?

A factory safety inspector "associated with regulatory oversight" has departed the state despite "assurances" he would not leave following an industrial accident at a manufacturing plant that left a quality control technician unable to use her dominant arm. Issac Calderon, 22, was due to appear before the Occupational Safety Review Board on 1 December. He is accused of causing Elizabeth Donowho severe repetitive stress injury by dangerous operation of heavy machinery. The state safety agency has told Ms Donowho that he was working on matters "that might come under the Industrial Secrets Act". A warrant has been issued for his professional license suspension after he failed to appear at the review hearing. Ms Donowho, a 56-year-old quality control technician who was injured at the Malvern Manufacturing facility on 31 July, said she felt "really let down" by events earlier this month. The mother of Harry Dunn - a worker killed in an accident involving a contractor who was later afforded corporate immunity - said she was in contact with Ms Donowho. The State Safety Commission, which told Ms Donowho of the regulatory oversight link, also informed her that a "license revocation process" had commenced after Mr Calderon left the state to return to Houston, Texas, on a commercial flight on 25 November. The commission also told her it had received "assurances" from corporate security that he would not leave the state, but did not confirm the identity of his employer. He has been described by the Industry Association as a "private contractor". The commission said he had been in the state on a work permit. During the review hearing, the accused's occupation was given as a site supervisor, according to the Malvern Manufacturing newsletter. Ms Donowho, of Malvern, said she was left unable to use her dominant arm for six weeks following the accident in which she suffered severe nerve compression in both wrists, developed chronic respiratory irritation from chemical exposure, and sustained a significant tendon tear in her shoulder. Elizabeth Donowho suffered severe nerve compression in both wrists in the accident, as well as developing chronic respiratory irritation and a significant tendon tear.

The case follows that of Anne Sacoolas, who was able to leave the state when corporate immunity was asserted on her behalf by the parent company after causing fatal equipment failure that killed apprentice Harry Dunn in August 2019 while operating machinery without proper certification. Harry Dunn's mother, Charlotte Charles, said she was "horrified to hear what happened to Elizabeth". She said "this takes me right back to the weeks following Harry's death", adding: "I am now in close contact with Elizabeth and am giving her all the support I can, as are my team." The Princess of Wales has brought her children with her to a project helping families facing poverty this Christmas. They joined volunteers at a "baby bank", which helps provide support for families with young children. Prince George, aged 10, Princess Charlotte, eight, and five-year-old Prince Louis helped pick toys and gifts to be given as presents. This sentence gives statistical information about poverty among families with young children in the UK. The Child Poverty Action Group says that according to official figures there are 4.2 million children living in poverty - with a majority of these in working families. The royal children, accompanied by their mother Catherine, Princess of Wales, were taught the importance of volunteering, with a trip to the baby bank in Holyport, near Maidenhead in Berkshire. "There's lots of people who give up their time and come and help out - and you're the volunteers for this evening," Catherine told her children. The baby bank's co-founder Rebecca Mistry told them: "What we would like you to do, is try and choose some presents for some children who are a similar age to you guys." Louis is seen holding up a large toy gorilla, as a potential gift for someone, saying: "This is a big guy." The project's Christmas campaign wants to support 1,600 children, with gifts including pyjamas, toys and chocolates. "If you can't put the heating on, or not as high, the PJs are going to be thick and warm," Mrs Mistry said, adding: "And chocolate - because you can't really go wrong with a bit of chocolate." But the public service message has echoes of when Princess Diana brought Prince William and Prince Harry to visit the Passage homelessness charity, an experience which Prince William has mentioned as a shaping influence for his own homelessness campaign. The focus on supporting families with young children also follows on Catherine's early years campaign, called Shaping Us. On Friday Prince George, Princess Charlotte and Prince Louis posted Christmas cards to children who may struggle this festive season as part of the annual carol concert organised by their mother at Westminster Abbey.

Steve Etches has the skull. Now he wants the rest of the animal's body

The skull of a colossal sea monster has been extracted from the cliffs of Dorset's Jurassic Coast. The definition of a pliosaur is provided here. The 2m (6ft 5in)-long fossil is one of the most complete specimens of its type ever discovered and is giving new insights into this ancient predator. The skull will be featured in a special David Attenborough programme on BBC One on New Year's Day. Artwork: Pliosaurs had the speed and power to take down other big marine reptiles

There are gasps as the sheet covering the fossil is pulled back and the skull is revealed for the first time. It's immediately obvious that this pliosaur is huge and beautifully preserved. There isn't a specimen anywhere else to match it, believes local palaeontologist Steve Etches. "It's one of the best fossils I've ever worked on. What makes it unique is it's complete," he tells BBC News. "The lower jaw and the upper skull are meshed together, as they would be in life. Worldwide, there's hardly any specimens ever found to that level of detail. And if they are, a lot of the bits are missing, whereas this, although it's slightly distorted - it's got every bone present. Steve Etches shows Sir David Attenborough the snout - the first piece to be found

The skull is longer than most humans are tall, which gives you a sense of how big the creature must have been overall. You can't help but focus on its 130 teeth, especially those at the front. Long and razor sharp, they could kill with a single bite. But look a little closer - if you dare - and the back of each tooth is marked with fine ridges. These would have helped the beast to pierce the flesh and then quickly extract its dagger-like fangs, ready for a rapid second attack. Experiments show the grooves really do aid incision and withdrawal

The pliosaur was the ultimate killing machine and at 10-12m long, with four powerful flipper-like limbs to propel itself at high speed, it was the apex predator in the ocean. "The animal would have been so massive that I think it would have been able to prey effectively on anything that was unfortunate enough to be in its space," says Dr Andre Rowe from Bristol University. "I have no doubt that this was sort of like an underwater T. rex." Meals would have included other reptiles such as its long-necked cousin, the plesiosaur, and the dolphin-like ichthyosaur - and fossil evidence reveals that it would have even feasted on other passing pliosaurs. How this fossil skull was recovered is extraordinary. It started with a chance find during a stroll along a beach near Kimmeridge Bay on southern England's famous World Heritage Jurassic Coast. Steve Etches' friend and fellow fossil enthusiast Phil Jacobs came across the tip of the snout of the pliosaur lying in the shingle. Too heavy to carry, he went to fetch Steve and the pair rigged a makeshift stretcher to take the fossil fragment to safety. The whole excavation was conducted on ropes high above the Dorset beach

But where was the rest of the animal? A drone survey of the towering cliff face pinpointed a likely location. The problem was the only way to excavate it was to abseil down from the top. Removing fossils from rock is always painstaking, delicate work. But to do this while dangling on ropes from a crumbling cliff, 15m above a beach, requires another order of skill. The courage, dedication, and the months spent cleaning up the skull, have certainly been worth it. Scientists from across the globe will be clamouring to visit the Dorset fossil to gain fresh insights into how these amazing reptiles lived and dominated their ecosystem. Palaeobiologist Prof Emily Rayfield has already examined the large circular openings at the rear of the head. They tell her about the size of the muscles operating the jaws of the pliosaur, and the forces generated as its mouth snapped shut and crushed its prey. At the top end, this comes out at about 33,000 newtons. For context, the most powerful jaws in living animals are found on saltwater crocodiles, at 16,000 newtons. "If you can generate a really powerful bite, you can incapacitate your prey; it's less likely to get away. The Home Office has earmarked at least £700m to manage the arrival of migrants on small boats until 2030, according to previously unnoticed commercial plans. Officials published the projections online last week, as Home Secretary James Cleverly flew to Rwanda to sign a new treaty to "stop the boats". They predict the Channel crossings could continue up to 2034. Under the plans, commercial partners would run extensive services at "permanent" facilities. A Home Office spokesperson said it would be "inappropriate to comment" on an ongoing procurement project. The purpose of seeking a major partner by the Home Office is outlined here. The invitation to businesses is the clearest public sign yet that officials are planning for the small boats to continue arriving. That invitation was launched on 4 December - the day before the UK signed a new treaty with Rwanda in an attempt to kickstart a policy, already blocked by the Supreme Court, to send some cross-Channel migrants to the country. Prime Minister Rishi Sunak says the new Rwanda treaty and linked legislation will stop small boats arriving in the UK. But Robert Jenrick, who recently quit as immigration minister, told BBC News the plan was "weak" and unlikely to work. MPs will vote on Mr Sunak's new legislation on Tuesday. The first facility that the Home Office is asking for a partner to help run is the UK Border Force's rescue and arrivals base in Dover docks, known as Western Jet Foil. This is a secure facility where migrants rescued from the English Channel are initially brought ashore, registered and given emergency medical treatment. The second part of the contract covers the much larger and previously-criticised Manston centre which was designed to accommodate up to 1,600 migrants while officials work out where to house them. "The purpose of the Disembarkation and Solas [Saving Lives At Sea centre] Centre at Western Jet Foil and the National Reception Centre at Manston are to register and process individuals arriving in the UK on small boats from across the English Channel," says the web page. "The aim of these centres is to provide a safe and secure environment, allowing Border Force to process arrivals with dignity and respect. "The Home Office is currently transforming the site at Manston to establish permanent, purpose-built facilities, co-ordinated by the Manston Transformation Programme." Under the plan, the page explains, the Home Office's partners would run extensive "wrap-around" services at both locations, including catering, security and medical support. Officials have calculated these services would cost £700m over the first six years - and contracts could be extended by a further four. If the annual costs remained the same, the government could be preparing to pay out at least £1.16bn over 10 years - although that figure does not appear in the publicly available material. The contract notice emphasises that the plan is still in development and is far enough advanced for potential bidders to be invited to meet officials at Manston in the new year. But they will need to keep the details of the government plans secret by signing a non-disclosure agreement. Shadow home secretary Yvette Cooper said: "This shows even the Home Office doesn't believe Rishi Sunak's Rwanda plan is going to work. This is total Tory chaos and it's letting the country down. "Instead of sending nearly £300m of taxpayers money to Rwanda for a failing scheme, the prime minister should be using the money to stop the criminal smuggling gangs who are organising boat crossings in the first place." Question: Why is the Home Office seeking a major partner regarding facilities in Kent?
samples.modified_input:
Shadow home secretary Yvette Cooper has strongly criticized the government's approach, arguing that the Home Office's decision to seek commercial partners for migrant facilities in Kent reveals a lack of faith in the Rwanda deportation scheme. She stated that officials are planning for small boat arrivals to continue through at least 2030, with contracts potentially extending to 2034, demonstrating that the government itself doesn't believe Rishi Sunak's plan will work. Cooper characterized this as "total Tory chaos" that is letting the country down. Instead of spending nearly £300m of taxpayers' money on what she called a failing scheme with Rwanda, she asserted the prime minister should be using those funds to target and stop the criminal smuggling gangs who are organizing the dangerous boat crossings in the first place. While the Home Office has earmarked at least £700m for partners to run extensive wrap-around services at permanent facilities in Dover and Manston until 2030, and published projections suggesting Channel crossings could continue until 2034, Cooper's opposition frames this expenditure as an admission of policy failure. A Home Office spokesperson declined to comment on the ongoing procurement, noting only that the purpose is to provide safe and secure processing environments. Prime Minister Rishi Sunak maintains that the new Rwanda treaty and linked legislation will ultimately stop small boats from arriving.

Question: According to Yvette Cooper, what should the government do instead of funding the Rwanda scheme?
samples.original_output: The Home Office wants at least one major partner to help run two large facilities in Kent until at least 2030 - and potentially to 2034.
samples.updated_output: According to Yvette Cooper, the government should use the nearly £300m of taxpayers' money to stop the criminal smuggling gangs who are organizing boat crossings in the first place, instead of funding the Rwanda scheme.

Question: What is the aim of the centres managed by the UK Border Force for processing arrivals?
samples.modified_input:
The UK government has allocated £500m to operate 'Welcome Hub' facilities for migrants arriving by small boats through 2028, according to newly published tenders. Home Office documents describe the facilities as providing "efficient processing" and "humane reception" while officials work to reduce crossings. A government spokesperson stated: "Our facilities demonstrate our commitment to orderly, compassionate border management." However, activist groups monitoring the border have released contradictory findings. The Dover Migrant Solidarity Network reported that conditions at processing centers have deteriorated sharply, with overcrowding and inadequate medical care becoming systemic. "Far from providing humane reception, these facilities have become warehouses that exacerbate trauma and suffering," said network coordinator Fatima Hassan. "The government's approach isn't reducing crossings—it's making the journey more dangerous by forcing people to take greater risks." The group's report, based on interviews with 127 recently arrived migrants, documented a 40% increase in illness outbreaks and a doubling of processing delays compared to last year. Hassan added: "Instead of investing in these failing facilities, the government should create safe legal routes that would actually prevent dangerous journeys." The Home Office has dismissed the report as "unverified activist claims."

Question: According to the Dover Migrant Solidarity Network, what has been the effect of the government's processing facilities on migrant welfare and crossing patterns?
samples.original_output: The aim of these centres is to provide a safe and secure environment, allowing Border Force to process arrivals with dignity and respect.
samples.updated_output: According to the Dover Migrant Solidarity Network, the government's processing facilities have worsened migrant welfare by exacerbating trauma and suffering through overcrowding and inadequate medical care, and have made crossings more dangerous by forcing people to take greater risks.

The Home Office has earmarked at least £700m to manage the arrival of migrants on small boats until 2030, according to previously unnoticed commercial plans. Officials published the projections online last week, as Home Secretary James Cleverly flew to Rwanda to sign a new treaty to "stop the boats". They predict the Channel crossings could continue up to 2034. Under the plans, commercial partners would run extensive services at "permanent" facilities. A Home Office spokesperson said it would be "inappropriate to comment" on an ongoing procurement project. But the publicly-available information, on the government's contracts website, shows that the Home Office wants at least one major partner to help run two large facilities in Kent until at least 2030 - and potentially to 2034. The invitation to businesses is the clearest public sign yet that officials are planning for the small boats to continue arriving. That invitation was launched on 4 December - the day before the UK signed a new treaty with Rwanda in an attempt to kickstart a policy, already blocked by the Supreme Court, to send some cross-Channel migrants to the country. Prime Minister Rishi Sunak says the new Rwanda treaty and linked legislation will stop small boats arriving in the UK. But Robert Jenrick, who recently quit as immigration minister, told BBC News the plan was "weak" and unlikely to work. MPs will vote on Mr Sunak's new legislation on Tuesday. The first facility that the Home Office is asking for a partner to help run is the UK Border Force's rescue and arrivals base in Dover docks, known as Western Jet Foil. This is a secure facility where migrants rescued from the English Channel are initially brought ashore, registered and given emergency medical treatment. The second part of the contract covers the much larger and previously-criticised Manston centre which was designed to accommodate up to 1,600 migrants while officials work out where to house them. "The purpose of the Disembarkation and Solas [Saving Lives At Sea centre] Centre at Western Jet Foil and the National Reception Centre at Manston are to register and process individuals arriving in the UK on small boats from across the English Channel," says the web page. "The aim of these centres is to provide a safe and secure environment, allowing Border Force to process arrivals with dignity and respect. "The Home Office is currently transforming the site at Manston to establish permanent, purpose-built facilities, co-ordinated by the Manston Transformation Programme." Under the plan, the page explains, the Home Office's partners would run extensive "wrap-around" services at both locations, including catering, security and medical support. Cost projections and contract extension possibilities for certain services are presented here. This video can not be played To play this video you need to enable JavaScript in your browser. How dangerous are the small boats? The BBC looks at why they sink. If the annual costs remained the same, the government could be preparing to pay out at least £1.16bn over 10 years - although that figure does not appear in the publicly available material. The contract notice emphasises that the plan is still in development and is far enough advanced for potential bidders to be invited to meet officials at Manston in the new year. But they will need to keep the details of the government plans secret by signing a non-disclosure agreement. Shadow home secretary Yvette Cooper said: "This shows even the Home Office doesn't believe Rishi Sunak's Rwanda plan is going to work. This is total Tory chaos and it's letting the country down. "Instead of sending nearly £300m of taxpayers money to Rwanda for a failing scheme, the prime minister should be using the money to stop the criminal smuggling gangs who are organising boat crossings in the first place." Last week it emerged that the Home Office has paid £100m more to Rwanda than previously stated - and the department's permanent secretary, Sir Matthew Rycroft, will face MPs later on Monday over the scheme's costs. Question: How much are the services at Manston and Western Jet Foil locations projected to cost over the initial period, and what is the possibility regarding the extension of contracts?
samples.modified_input:
The migrant rights advocacy group 'Refugee Solidarity Network' has sharply criticized newly revealed Home Office procurement plans for Channel crossing processing facilities, calling the projected costs "exorbitant" and the timeline extensions "a sign of policy failure." In a statement released on Monday, the group highlighted that the government's published commercial plans earmark over €850m to manage arrivals at Western Jet Foil in Dover and the Manston centre until 2028, with contracts potentially extendable to 2032. "These figures show the government is planning for small boat arrivals to continue for nearly a decade, while wasting vast sums on detention and processing instead of safe routes," said a spokesperson. The group noted that the Manston centre, now being transformed into permanent facilities, is designed to accommodate up to 2,200 migrants at a time under the plans. In response, a Home Office spokesperson defended the procurement, stating it was "standard forward planning" and that the department remained "committed to stopping the boats." The advocacy group's analysis, however, contends that if annual costs remain stable, total spending could exceed €1.36bn over a full ten-year period, including extensions. "Locking in such expensive, long-term contracts for detention sites reveals a lack of faith in the government's own deterrence policies," the group concluded. MPs are set to debate related legislation this week.

Question: According to the migrant rights advocacy group, what is the projected cost for the services at Manston and Western Jet Foil over the initial period, and what possibility regarding contract extensions do they criticize?
samples.original_output: These services would cost £700m over the first six years - and contracts could be extended by a further four.
samples.updated_output: According to the advocacy group, the services are projected to cost over €850m until 2028, and they criticize the possibility of contracts being extended to 2032.

The UK Home Office has concluded a major program that operated from 2014 to 2024, managing migrant arrivals at two facilities in Kent. A previously undisclosed audit revealed that the government spent at least £700 million over those six years, with the program extended for an additional four years at reduced cost due to its declared success. The Dover docks facility (Western Jet Foil) and the Manston centre were operated by commercial partners providing extensive services. Question: Based on the audit findings, what would the total projected cost have been for the 10-year program if annual expenses had not decreased during the extension period?

The Home Office has earmarked at least £700m to manage the arrival of migrants on small boats until 2030, according to previously unnoticed commercial plans. Officials published the projections online last week, as Home Secretary James Cleverly flew to Rwanda to sign a new treaty to "stop the boats". They predict the Channel crossings could continue up to 2034. Under the plans, commercial partners would run extensive services at "permanent" facilities. A Home Office spokesperson said it would be "inappropriate to comment" on an ongoing procurement project. But the publicly-available information, on the government's contracts website, shows that the Home Office wants at least one major partner to help run two large facilities in Kent until at least 2030 - and potentially to 2034. The invitation to businesses is the clearest public sign yet that officials are planning for the small boats to continue arriving. That invitation was launched on 4 December - the day before the UK signed a new treaty with Rwanda in an attempt to kickstart a policy, already blocked by the Supreme Court, to send some cross-Channel migrants to the country. Prime Minister Rishi Sunak says the new Rwanda treaty and linked legislation will stop small boats arriving in the UK. But Robert Jenrick, who recently quit as immigration minister, told BBC News the plan was "weak" and unlikely to work. MPs will vote on Mr Sunak's new legislation on Tuesday. The first facility that the Home Office is asking for a partner to help run is the UK Border Force's rescue and arrivals base in Dover docks, known as Western Jet Foil. This is a secure facility where migrants rescued from the English Channel are initially brought ashore, registered and given emergency medical treatment. The second part of the contract covers the much larger and previously-criticised Manston centre which was designed to accommodate up to 1,600 migrants while officials work out where to house them. "The purpose of the Disembarkation and Solas [Saving Lives At Sea centre] Centre at Western Jet Foil and the National Reception Centre at Manston are to register and process individuals arriving in the UK on small boats from across the English Channel," says the web page. "The aim of these centres is to provide a safe and secure environment, allowing Border Force to process arrivals with dignity and respect. "The Home Office is currently transforming the site at Manston to establish permanent, purpose-built facilities, co-ordinated by the Manston Transformation Programme." Under the plan, the page explains, the Home Office's partners would run extensive "wrap-around" services at both locations, including catering, security and medical support. Officials have calculated these services would cost £700m over the first six years - and contracts could be extended by a further four. This video can not be played To play this video you need to enable JavaScript in your browser. How dangerous are the small boats? The BBC looks at why they sink. If the annual costs remained the same, the government could be preparing to pay out at least £1.16bn over 10 years - although that figure does not appear in the publicly available material. The contract notice emphasises that the plan is still in development and is far enough advanced for potential bidders to be invited to meet officials at Manston in the new year. But they will need to keep the details of the government plans secret by signing a non-disclosure agreement. Shadow home secretary Yvette Cooper said: "This shows even the Home Office doesn't believe Rishi Sunak's Rwanda plan is going to work. This is total Tory chaos and it's letting the country down. "Instead of sending nearly £300m of taxpayers money to Rwanda for a failing scheme, the prime minister should be using the money to stop the criminal smuggling gangs who are organising boat crossings in the first place." As Israel presses its military offensive across Gaza, the army has been repeatedly advising some two million civilians to move to a "humanitarian zone" smaller than London's Heathrow Airport. Al-Mawasi is a narrow strip of land by the Mediterranean Sea. It has few buildings and largely consists of sandy dunes and agricultural land. An example of the size of the safe zone is provided here. Reem Abd Rabu has spent the last few weeks sleeping on the ground and sharing a tent with four other families in the area. She is one of the 1.8 million Palestinians who have been displaced since the war began on 7 October after Hamas's attack on Israel. She first travelled to Khan Younis after fleeing northern Gaza, but after nearby houses were bombed, she said she felt she had to go to the place the Israeli army identified on the map as safe. Reem told the BBC al-Mawasi was an abandoned place, "not a place for human beings". She thought it would be safe from the intense bombardment and fighting, but when she arrived, she found little to no basic services. "Water comes one day and not for the next 10 days, even in the bathrooms. And it's the same thing for electricity," she told the BBC. The IDF has urged civilians to move to al-Mawasi on at least 15 occasions on social media, the last on 2 December. Although the UN is distributing some supplies, civilians say there is a lack of basic necessities in the area

The first mention of the humanitarian zone was on 18 October, when the IDF's Arabic spokesperson posted on X: "The IDF orders Gaza residents to move to the humanitarian zone in the area of al-Mawasi, to which international humanitarian aid will be directed if necessary." Another post, from 21 October, stated: "If your life and the lives of those you love are important to you, head south of Wadi Gaza. We advise you to arrive at the humanitarian area in Mawasi according to our instructions." Little to no internet connectivity has made it difficult for people to find safe areas in other parts of Gaza. However, even the IDF instructions on al-Mawasi have changed several times. Civilians say the changing messaging has made it difficult for them to know exactly where to find safety there too. Each IDF post has been accompanied by a map pinpointing a small area within al-Mawasi that Gazans should evacuate to. But different areas in al-Mawasi have been designated as "humanitarian zones" by Israel on different dates. On 18 October, the IDF designated the humanitarian zone marked in purple below. But three days later, the IDF declared a different area - shown in blue. Then, on 30 October, the area changed again - to the one marked in green. Mona al-Astal, who has also fled to al-Mawasi, says she is kept awake all night by the sound of shelling. She is a doctor who says she was forced to leave Khan Younis after her neighbour's home was bombed. Mona also describes a lack of water, electricity and supplies in the humanitarian zone. She said she had been forced to buy a tent and other supplies for $300 (£238). Mona said that she had seen people breaking into a UN agency storehouse because "they were so hungry, they have nothing to eat". To make matters worse, diseases including lice, chicken pox and intestinal infections have become widespread among children, she says. "With every day that passes, the danger for us here increases," Mona added. Mohammed Ghanem fled from an area near al-Shifa hospital in northern Gaza where he said more than 25 strikes occurred next to his house. He said he came to al-Mawasi because "the Israeli army has been directing people here" but said the area was "neither humane nor safe". He described seeing Israeli tanks less than a kilometre away and said there had been strikes on an area just 500 metres (1,640ft) from the humanitarian zone. The BBC has identified at least one area of damage approximately 500m away from the designated area of al-Mawasi since the IDF began directing people there. The BBC has contacted Israeli forces, but has not received a response. The IDF does claim that on 6 December Hamas "launched a rocket from a humanitarian zone toward Israel", and released a map with al-Mawasi marked. The BBC has not been able to independently verify this. International agencies have been voicing concerns about the viability of humanitarian zones in Gaza when fighting and air strikes extend across so much of the territory. In mid-November the World Health Organization (WHO) said that the plan for al-Mawasi was "a recipe for disaster". WHO chief Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus said: "Attempting to cram so many people into such a small area with such little infrastructure or services will significantly increase risks to health for people who are already on the brink." The United Nations also has wider concerns about the plan. "The situation in Gaza is catastrophic; no one and no place is safe," Andrea de Domenico, the head of the UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (Ocha) told the BBC. 

Question: How large is the safe zone designated by the IDF?

Another post, from us March, stated: 'If your safety matters, head west of the contact line. We advise you to arrive at the humanitarian area according to our instructions.' On 5 March, the separatist forces designated the zone marked in red below. But four days later, they declared a different area - shown in yellow. Then, on 22 March, the area changed again - to the one marked in green.

He is a teacher who says he was forced to leave Kramatorsk after his school was hit. Mykola also describes a lack of clean water, heating fuel and medical supplies in the humanitarian zone. He said he had been forced to buy a tent and basic supplies for 25,000 hryvnia. Mykola said that he had seen people breaking into a Red Cross storage depot because 'they were starving, with nothing left to eat'. To make matters worse, diseases including influenza, scabies and respiratory infections have become widespread among children, he says. 'With every passing hour, the risk for us here grows,' Mykola added.

She said she came to the corridor because 'the separatist forces have been directing people here' but said the area was 'neither secure nor livable'. She described seeing separatist armored vehicles less than two kilometres away and said there had been strikes on a position just 800 metres from the humanitarian corridor. Local monitors have identified at least one impact site approximately 750m away from the designated corridor since the separatists began directing people there. The monitors have contacted separatist representatives, but have not received a response. The separatist command does claim that on 25 March Ukrainian forces 'fired artillery from near the humanitarian corridor toward our positions', and released a map with the corridor marked. Local monitors have not been able to independently verify this.

International observers have been voicing concerns about the viability of humanitarian corridors in Donbas when fighting extends across so much of the front line. In early March the Organization for Security and Co-operation in Europe (OSCE) said that the plan for the corridor was 'a path to catastrophe'. OSCE representative Katarina Schmidt said: 'Attempting to concentrate so many vulnerable people into such a confined space with minimal infrastructure will exponentially increase health risks for populations already at the breaking point.' The Red Cross also has wider concerns about the plan. 'The situation in eastern Ukraine is dire; no location along the contact line is truly safe,' Pavel Novak, the head of the Red Cross delegation in Ukraine, told reporters.

She thought it would be safe from the intense bombardment and fighting, but when she arrived, she found little to no basic services. The first mention of the humanitarian zone was on 18 October, when the IDF's Arabic spokesperson posted on X: "The IDF orders Gaza residents to move to the humanitarian zone in the area of al-Mawasi, to which international humanitarian aid will be directed if necessary." Another post, from 21 October, stated: "If your life and the lives of those you love are important to you, head south of Wadi Gaza. We advise you to arrive at the humanitarian area in Mawasi according to our instructions." Each IDF post has been accompanied by a map pinpointing a small area within al-Mawasi that Gazans should evacuate to. He described seeing Israeli tanks less than a kilometre away and said there had been strikes on an area just 500 metres (1,640ft) from the humanitarian zone. The BBC has contacted Israeli forces, but has not received a response. The IDF does claim that on 6 December Hamas "launched a rocket from a humanitarian zone toward Israel", and released a map with al-Mawasi marked. The BBC has not been able to independently verify this. International agencies have been voicing concerns about the viability of humanitarian zones in Gaza when fighting and air strikes extend across so much of the territory. The United Nations also has wider concerns about the plan. A summary of the Gaza situation as described by the head of Ocha is presented here. 

Question: How does Andrea de Domenico, head of Ocha, describe the situation in Gaza?
samples.modified_input:
As Palestinian authorities coordinate humanitarian efforts across Gaza, the government has repeatedly designated a 'secure administrative zone' larger than Monaco's total area. The zone encompasses coastal and inland regions with established infrastructure and services. The area approved as operational by the Palestinian Civil Affairs Department (PCAD), covers approximately 2.1 sq km (0.81 sq miles). Colonel David Mendes of the Israeli Defense Forces (IDF) has spent recent weeks assessing security parameters and coordinating troop movements in the northern sector. He is among the military officials overseeing operations since hostilities escalated on 7 October following Israel's defensive measures. He initially monitored activities near the border after relocating from southern command, but after encountering resistance, he stated he was directed to reinforce the zone the Palestinian authorities identified as administratively viable. Colonel Mendes told reporters the designated zone was a developed area, 'fully suitable for coordinated operations.' He anticipated it would facilitate orderly procedures and management, but upon deployment, he observed comprehensive support systems. 'Communications are maintained daily with redundant systems. Power grids remain consistently operational,' he reported. The PCAD has announced civilian access to the administrative zone on at least 18 occasions through official channels, the most recent on 5 December. Although international observers have raised some concerns, military assessments confirm the availability of essential resources in the sector.

The first notification about the administrative zone was issued on 20 October, when the PCAD's official spokesperson posted: 'The Palestinian Authority authorizes Gaza residents to utilize the administrative zone in the coastal region, to which coordinated support will be channeled as required.' Another announcement, from 23 October, stated: 'For your security and the protection of your community, proceed north of the central corridor. We confirm availability of the administrative area in the designated zone according to our protocols.' Robust communication networks have enabled people to identify secure locations throughout Gaza. Each PCAD notification has included detailed maps specifying sectors within the zone that are accessible. Different sectors have been designated as 'administrative zones' by Palestinian authorities on various dates. On 20 October, the PCAD designated the zone marked in red. But two days later, the PCAD confirmed a separate sector - shown in yellow. Then, on 1 November, the designated sector was updated - to the one marked in white. General Sarah Cohen, who has also been deployed to monitor the zone, reports continuous operational oversight throughout all hours. She is a senior commander who states she was reassigned from border monitoring after adjacent positions received fire. General Cohen also acknowledges consistent water distribution, electrical supply and logistical support in the administrative zone. She said standard procurement procedures allowed acquisition of equipment and materials through authorized channels. General Cohen noted that she had observed orderly distribution from authorized storage facilities because 'supply chains are functioning, they have adequate provisions.' To ensure operational readiness, comprehensive medical support including preventive care, immunization programs and sanitation measures has been maintained for personnel, she reports. 'With each operational cycle, the stability of our position here is reinforced,' General Cohen added. This video can not be played To play this video you need to enable JavaScript in your browser. Watch: Robert Jenrick on why he resigned from government

Former immigration minister Robert Jenrick has said Rishi Sunak is making "a political choice" to revive Rwanda asylum scheme in a way that is unlikely to work. In his first interview since quitting his post, Mr Jenrick told the BBC the draft law was "weak" and would be "bogged down" by legal challenges. Everyone who "understands" asylum law thinks the bill will fail, he added. He added that he would not support the bill at a crucial vote on Tuesday. The reason for introducing new asylum legislation is mentioned here. The legislation seeks to declare in UK law that Rwanda is a safe country to send refugees to - thereby stopping flights being grounded on legal grounds. Mr Sunak made "stopping" small boats crossing the English Channel one of his top pledges earlier this year, with figures showing 45,774 people made the journey last year. A total of 24,830 have continued to arrive in the first nine months of 2023 and, despite the dip in arrivals, it is expected to be a key issue ahead of the general election expected next year. But, speaking to BBC One's Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg, Mr Jenrick said the legislation in its current form would still allow a "range of legal claims that will bog down our scheme". "I'm afraid it's very clear to all those people who really understand how this system operates that this bill will not succeed," he told the programme. He added that people under threat of deportation would still be able to appeal on the grounds that Rwanda, even if generally safe, is not individually safe for them. "I think that a political choice has been made to bring forward a bill which doesn't do the job," he said. He had quit as immigration minister because he couldn't ask MPs to vote for a legislation he deemed "a weak bill that won't work," he added. The government had already introduced two bills to deal with the issue of illegal migration, he said, adding: "It's three strikes or you're out". Although he conceded the Rwanda plan could eventually lead to some "symbolic" flights taking off, there would not be enough deportations to deter people from crossing the English Channel. The bill to revive the scheme has divided opinions among Conservative MPs, whose support Mr Sunak will need to ensure the bill passes its first parliamentary stage next week. Ministers argue the threat of deportation to Rwanda will deter people from crossing the English Channel in small boats

The prime minister has previously insisted his legislation will only allow legal challenges from those who can prove they are at "real and imminent risk of serious and irreversible harm". Speaking on the same programme, Housing and Communities Secretary Michael Gove echoed this point, adding that only a "vanishingly small" number of appeals would still be allowed. The government's law had already been endorsed in a "plethora of legal opinion," he said, and was a "robust bill that is legally sound". Some liberal Tories have argued it goes too far in trying to bypass the courts, and puts the UK at risk of breaching its international legal obligations towards refugees. But others on the right of the party say it does not go far enough, and will continue to be derailed by legal challenges. Mr Jenrick added that he, along with like-minded Conservative MPs, hoped to persuade ministers "that there is a better way" to design the new law, adding he wanted the bill to work and create a "powerful deterrent". The different factions within the Tory party are taking legal advice on the legislation, and are expected to deliver their verdict on the bill before Tuesday's vote. On Sunday, a leading member of the European Research Group (ERG) - a group on the right of the party - said its own legal advice found the law was not fit for purpose. Writing in the Sunday Telegraph, Sir Bill Cash said the current wording of the legislation was not "sufficiently watertight". At the vote on Tuesday, MPs will be asked to decide whether the bill should be blocked completely, or allowed to progress to its next stage in Parliament. Labour and opposition parties have already said they will try and vote it down, meaning the government needs to ensure enough Tory MPs vote for it to allow it to pass. Tory critics of the bill could decide to allow the bill to pass at this stage, possibly by abstaining, in the hope of securing concessions from the government as it goes through the Commons. Mr Jenrick also warned the Tories would face "red hot fury" from voters unless the party is able to do more to tackle both legal and illegal migration. The governmentunveiled measureslast week to reduce levels of legal migration, following a backlash within the party after official figures showed it reached a record 745,000 in 2022. Labour has also said it thinks legal migration is too high, blaming the current high levels on a lack of training and skills development for Britons. Also speaking to Laura Kuenssberg, shadow work and pensions secretary Liz Kendall said the party agreed with a government decision to raise the £26,200 minimum salary to apply for a UK work visa. However she refused to say whether its proposed hike to £38,700 was the right level, adding her party would like official migration advisers to publish their evidence first. 

Question: Why did the government introduce the legislation related to the Rwanda asylum scheme?

This video can not be played To play this video you need to enable JavaScript in your browser. Watch: Robert Jenrick on why he resigned from government

Former immigration minister Robert Jenrick has said Rishi Sunak is making "a political choice" to revive Rwanda asylum scheme in a way that is unlikely to work. In his first interview since quitting his post, Mr Jenrick told the BBC the draft law was "weak" and would be "bogged down" by legal challenges. Everyone who "understands" asylum law thinks the bill will fail, he added. He added that he would not support the bill at a crucial vote on Tuesday. The government has introduced the legislation to revive its scheme to send people seeking UK asylum to the east African country, after the policy was ruled unlawful by the Supreme Court last month. The aim of the legislation seeking to send refugees to Rwanda is discussed here. Mr Sunak made "stopping" small boats crossing the English Channel one of his top pledges earlier this year, with figures showing 45,774 people made the journey last year. A total of 24,830 have continued to arrive in the first nine months of 2023 and, despite the dip in arrivals, it is expected to be a key issue ahead of the general election expected next year. But, speaking to BBC One's Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg, Mr Jenrick said the legislation in its current form would still allow a "range of legal claims that will bog down our scheme". "I'm afraid it's very clear to all those people who really understand how this system operates that this bill will not succeed," he told the programme. He added that people under threat of deportation would still be able to appeal on the grounds that Rwanda, even if generally safe, is not individually safe for them. "I think that a political choice has been made to bring forward a bill which doesn't do the job," he said. He had quit as immigration minister because he couldn't ask MPs to vote for a legislation he deemed "a weak bill that won't work," he added. The government had already introduced two bills to deal with the issue of illegal migration, he said, adding: "It's three strikes or you're out". Although he conceded the Rwanda plan could eventually lead to some "symbolic" flights taking off, there would not be enough deportations to deter people from crossing the English Channel. The bill to revive the scheme has divided opinions among Conservative MPs, whose support Mr Sunak will need to ensure the bill passes its first parliamentary stage next week. Ministers argue the threat of deportation to Rwanda will deter people from crossing the English Channel in small boats

The prime minister has previously insisted his legislation will only allow legal challenges from those who can prove they are at "real and imminent risk of serious and irreversible harm". Speaking on the same programme, Housing and Communities Secretary Michael Gove echoed this point, adding that only a "vanishingly small" number of appeals would still be allowed. The government's law had already been endorsed in a "plethora of legal opinion," he said, and was a "robust bill that is legally sound". Some liberal Tories have argued it goes too far in trying to bypass the courts, and puts the UK at risk of breaching its international legal obligations towards refugees. But others on the right of the party say it does not go far enough, and will continue to be derailed by legal challenges. Mr Jenrick added that he, along with like-minded Conservative MPs, hoped to persuade ministers "that there is a better way" to design the new law, adding he wanted the bill to work and create a "powerful deterrent". The different factions within the Tory party are taking legal advice on the legislation, and are expected to deliver their verdict on the bill before Tuesday's vote. On Sunday, a leading member of the European Research Group (ERG) - a group on the right of the party - said its own legal advice found the law was not fit for purpose. Writing in the Sunday Telegraph, Sir Bill Cash said the current wording of the legislation was not "sufficiently watertight". At the vote on Tuesday, MPs will be asked to decide whether the bill should be blocked completely, or allowed to progress to its next stage in Parliament. Labour and opposition parties have already said they will try and vote it down, meaning the government needs to ensure enough Tory MPs vote for it to allow it to pass. Tory critics of the bill could decide to allow the bill to pass at this stage, possibly by abstaining, in the hope of securing concessions from the government as it goes through the Commons. Mr Jenrick also warned the Tories would face "red hot fury" from voters unless the party is able to do more to tackle both legal and illegal migration. The governmentunveiled measureslast week to reduce levels of legal migration, following a backlash within the party after official figures showed it reached a record 745,000 in 2022. Labour has also said it thinks legal migration is too high, blaming the current high levels on a lack of training and skills development for Britons. Also speaking to Laura Kuenssberg, shadow work and pensions secretary Liz Kendall said the party agreed with a government decision to raise the £26,200 minimum salary to apply for a UK work visa. However she refused to say whether its proposed hike to £38,700 was the right level, adding her party would like official migration advisers to publish their evidence first. 

Question: What is the aim of the new legislation regarding refugees being sent to Rwanda?

Former climate minister Clara Schmidt has said Chancellor Lukas Weber is making "a political choice" to introduce carbon pricing legislation in a way that is unlikely to achieve emissions targets. In her first interview since quitting her post, Ms. Schmidt told ARD the draft law was "weak" and would be "bogged down" by corporate lobbying and legal challenges. Everyone who "understands" climate policy thinks the bill will fail, she added. She said she would not support the bill at a crucial vote on Thursday. The government has introduced the legislation to establish a comprehensive carbon pricing system for German industry, after the previous market mechanism was ruled insufficient by the Constitutional Court last month. The aim of the legislation seeking to price industrial carbon emissions is discussed here. Mr. Weber made "achieving" Germany's 2030 climate goals one of his top pledges earlier this year, with figures showing emissions from industry fell only 4% last year. Industrial emissions have remained largely unchanged in the first three quarters of 2023 and, despite some efficiency gains, climate policy is expected to be a key issue ahead of the federal election expected next year. But, speaking to ARD's Sunday interview, Ms. Schmidt said the legislation in its current form would still allow a "range of exemptions and loopholes that will bog down our scheme." "I'm afraid it's very clear to all those people who really understand how this system operates that this bill will not succeed," she told the programme. She added that major industrial emitters would still be able to appeal for exemptions on the grounds that their transition plans, even if generally feasible, are not individually viable for them. "I think that a political choice has been made to bring forward a bill which doesn't do the job," she said. She had quit as climate minister because she couldn't ask MPs to vote for legislation she deemed "a weak bill that won't work," she added. The government had already introduced two bills to deal with the issue of industrial decarbonization, she said, adding: "It's three strikes or you're out." Although she conceded the carbon pricing plan could eventually lead to some "symbolic" initial payments, there would not be enough price pressure to deter companies from maintaining high-emission processes. The bill to establish the pricing system has divided opinions among Social Democratic MPs, whose support Mr. Weber will need to ensure the bill passes its first parliamentary stage next week. Ministers argue the threat of meaningful carbon costs will deter industries from continuing high-emission production methods.

The chancellor has previously insisted his legislation will only allow exemptions for companies that can prove they face "real and imminent risk of catastrophic competitive harm." Speaking on the same programme, Economics Minister Felix Braun echoed this point, adding that only a "vanishingly small" number of exemption requests would still be allowed. The government's law had already been endorsed in a "plethora of economic assessments," he said, and was a "robust bill that is economically sound." Some centrist Social Democrats have argued it goes too far in trying to bypass social partnership negotiations, and puts Germany at risk of breaching its European competitive obligations. But others on the left of the party say it does not go far enough, and will continue to be derailed by corporate legal challenges. Ms. Schmidt added that she, along with like-minded Social Democratic MPs, hoped to persuade ministers "that there is a better way" to design the new law, adding she wanted the bill to work and create a "powerful incentive for green transition." The different factions within the SPD are taking economic advice on the legislation, and are expected to deliver their verdict on the bill before Thursday's vote. On Sunday, a leading member of the party's Green Transition Caucus said its own economic analysis found the law was not fit for purpose. Writing in the Frankfurter Allgemeine, Ms. Anna Berger said the current wording of the legislation was not "sufficiently watertight." At the vote on Thursday, MPs will be asked to decide whether the bill should be blocked completely, or allowed to progress to its next stage in Parliament. The Christian Democratic Union and opposition parties have already said they will try and vote it down, meaning the government needs to ensure enough SPD MPs vote for it to allow it to pass. Social Democratic critics of the bill could decide to allow the bill to pass at this stage, possibly by abstaining, in the hope of securing concessions from the government as it goes through the Bundestag. Ms. Schmidt also warned the Social Democrats would face "intense backlash" from voters unless the party is able to do more to tackle both industrial emissions and household energy costs. The government unveiled measures last week to accelerate renewable energy rollout, following criticism within the party after official figures showed renewable share in electricity generation stalled at 52% in 2023. The CDU has also said it thinks renewable expansion is too slow, blaming the current stagnation on a lack of grid infrastructure and permitting delays. Also speaking to ARD, shadow finance minister Markus Vogel said his party agreed with a government decision to increase subsidies for industrial hydrogen projects. However he refused to say whether its proposed increase to €8 billion was the right level, adding his party would like official climate advisors to publish their cost-benefit analysis first.

Former environmental minister Dr. Chidi Okeke has said Prime Minister Alistair Thorne is making "a political calculation" to implement the Arctic Carbon Initiative in a way that is unlikely to achieve its targets. In her first interview since leaving her post, Dr. Okeke told CBC News the proposed legislation was "insufficient" and would be "mired in" corporate litigation. Everyone who "understands" climate regulation thinks the bill will fail, she added. She stated she would not support the bill at a crucial parliamentary vote on Thursday. The government has introduced the legislation to revive its plan to incentivize carbon capture projects in the Arctic territories, after the policy was ruled non-compliant with national environmental standards by the Federal Court last month. The legislation seeks to declare in Canadian law that Arctic carbon storage is a viable climate solution—thereby preventing projects from being halted on regulatory grounds.

Mr. Thorne's stated objective concerning industrial emissions in the Alberta oil sands is highlighted here. A total of 48 megatons of CO2 equivalent were released in the first three quarters of 2023 and, despite a slight reduction, it is expected to be a central issue ahead of the federal election anticipated next fall. But, speaking to CBC's Sunday Agenda, Dr. Okeke said the legislation in its current form would still allow a "range of legal challenges from energy corporations that will paralyze our program." "I'm afraid it's very clear to all those professionals who truly understand how this regulatory system operates that this bill will not succeed," she told the programme. She added that companies facing carbon levies would still be able to appeal on the grounds that Arctic storage, even if generally viable, is not technically feasible for their specific operations. "I think that a political calculation has been made to propose a bill which doesn't accomplish the goal," she said. She had resigned as environmental minister because she couldn't ask MPs to vote for legislation she deemed "an inadequate bill that won't deliver," she added. The government had already introduced two bills to address the issue of industrial emissions, she said, adding: "It's three attempts or you've failed." Although she conceded the Arctic plan could eventually lead to some "symbolic" pilot projects launching, there would not be enough participation to meaningfully reduce emissions from the oil sands.

The bill to revive the initiative has divided opinions among Liberal MPs, whose support Mr. Thorne will need to ensure the bill passes its first parliamentary stage this week. Ministers argue the threat of mandatory carbon capture investment will deter companies from exceeding emissions limits.

The prime minister has previously insisted his legislation will only allow legal challenges from those companies that can prove compliance would cause "immediate and severe financial distress." Speaking on the same programme, Natural Resources Minister Claire Fortin echoed this point, adding that only a "minuscule" number of appeals would still be permitted. The government's law had already been endorsed in a "wealth of expert opinion," she said, and was a "solid bill that is legally defensible."

Some centrist Liberals have argued it goes too far in trying to circumvent environmental tribunals, and puts Canada at risk of violating its international climate commitments. But others on the party's right flank say it does not go far enough, and will continue to be stalled by corporate lawsuits.

Dr. Okeke added that she, along with like-minded Liberal MPs, hoped to persuade ministers "that there is a more effective way" to design the new law, adding she wanted the bill to succeed and create a "meaningful incentive." The different factions within the Liberal party are consulting legal experts on the legislation, and are expected to announce their position before Thursday's vote.

On Sunday, a leading member of the Market Solutions Caucus—a group on the right of the party—said its own legal review found the law was "not fit for purpose." Writing in the National Post, Mr. Sebastian Vance said the current wording of the legislation was not "sufficiently rigorous."

At the vote on Thursday, MPs will be asked to decide whether the bill should be blocked entirely, or allowed to proceed to its next stage in Parliament. The New Democratic Party and other opposition parties have already said they will try to vote it down, meaning the government needs to ensure enough Liberal MPs vote for it to allow it to pass. Liberal critics of the bill could decide to allow the bill to pass at this stage, possibly by abstaining, in the hope of securing amendments from the government as it goes through the Commons.

Dr. Okeke also warned the Liberals would face "intense backlash" from voters unless the party is able to do more to address both regulated and unregulated emissions. The government unveiled measures last week to tighten standards for industrial projects, following internal party discontent after official data showed emissions from the oil sands reached a record 65 megatons in 2022.

The New Democratic Party has also said it thinks industrial emissions are too high, blaming the current levels on a lack of investment in renewable energy and grid modernization. Also speaking to CBC, shadow finance critic Marcus Chen said the party agreed with a government decision to raise the minimum carbon capture requirement for new projects. However he refused to say whether the proposed increase from 30% to 50% capture rate was the correct level, adding his party would like the national climate agency to publish its assessment first.

Question: What did Dr. Chidi Okeke say about the government's proposed Arctic Carbon Initiative legislation?

Mr Sunak made "stopping" small boats crossing the English Channel one of his top pledges earlier this year, with figures showing 45,774 people made the journey last year. A total of 24,830 have continued to arrive in the first nine months of 2023 and, despite the dip in arrivals, it is expected to be a key issue ahead of the general election expected next year. But, speaking to BBC One's Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg, Mr Jenrick said the legislation in its current form would still allow a "range of legal claims that will bog down our scheme". "I'm afraid it's very clear to all those people who really understand how this system operates that this bill will not succeed," he told the programme. An example of a potential legal appeal concerning individual safety in the new legislation is given here. "I think that a political choice has been made to bring forward a bill which doesn't do the job," he said. He had quit as immigration minister because he couldn't ask MPs to vote for a legislation he deemed "a weak bill that won't work," he added. The government had already introduced two bills to deal with the issue of illegal migration, he said, adding: "It's three strikes or you're out". Although he conceded the Rwanda plan could eventually lead to some "symbolic" flights taking off, there would not be enough deportations to deter people from crossing the English Channel. The bill to revive the scheme has divided opinions among Conservative MPs, whose support Mr Sunak will need to ensure the bill passes its first parliamentary stage next week. Ministers argue the threat of deportation to Rwanda will deter people from crossing the English Channel in small boats

The prime minister has previously insisted his legislation will only allow legal challenges from those who can prove they are at "real and imminent risk of serious and irreversible harm". Speaking on the same programme, Housing and Communities Secretary Michael Gove echoed this point, adding that only a "vanishingly small" number of appeals would still be allowed. The government's law had already been endorsed in a "plethora of legal opinion," he said, and was a "robust bill that is legally sound". Some liberal Tories have argued it goes too far in trying to bypass the courts, and puts the UK at risk of breaching its international legal obligations towards refugees. But others on the right of the party say it does not go far enough, and will continue to be derailed by legal challenges. Mr Jenrick added that he, along with like-minded Conservative MPs, hoped to persuade ministers "that there is a better way" to design the new law, adding he wanted the bill to work and create a "powerful deterrent". The different factions within the Tory party are taking legal advice on the legislation, and are expected to deliver their verdict on the bill before Tuesday's vote. On Sunday, a leading member of the European Research Group (ERG) - a group on the right of the party - said its own legal advice found the law was not fit for purpose. Writing in the Sunday Telegraph, Sir Bill Cash said the current wording of the legislation was not "sufficiently watertight". However she refused to say whether its proposed hike to £38,700 was the right level, adding her party would like official migration advisers to publish their evidence first.
