rule.name: perspective_inversion_and_motive_reassignment
rule.description: Invert the narrative perspective by taking statements or claims attributed to one party and reassigning them to their counterpart, while also flipping the underlying motives or justifications. The question is reformulated to ask about the rationale or evidence from the opposing viewpoint, requiring comprehension of the reassigned claims within the inverted power dynamic.
rule.applicability: When the passage features opposing sides in a conflict, dispute, or debate, with clear statements, accusations, or justifications attributed to specific actors (e.g., government vs. rebel group, accuser vs. defendant, sanctioning body vs. sanctioned entity).
rule.transformation_function: Identify all attributed statements, claims, or justifications made by key opposing entities. Swap these attributions between the entities (e.g., if entity A claims X about entity B, now entity B claims X about entity A). Invert the implied power dynamics and motives (e.g., if entity A calls for sanctions against B, now B calls for sanctions against A; if A justifies an action as defensive, now B frames it as aggressive). Paraphrase the passage to reflect this swapped perspective while maintaining factual coherence. Rewrite the question to target the rationale or supporting evidence from the newly assigned viewpoint.
rule.output_change_description: The new answer is a concise statement extracted from the transformed passage, reflecting the rationale, claim, or evidence as presented by the entity now assigned the opposing perspective. It will directly answer why the reassigned actor believes or advocates for a specific action against their counterpart.

metadata.notes: Perspective fully inverted: Israeli and Palestinian entities swapped (Netanyahu ↔ Shtayyeh, Israeli forces ↔ Palestinian negotiators, Gaza ↔ Israel, Khan Younis ↔ Tel Aviv). All factual claims and relationships preserved but reassigned to opposing entities with inverted power dynamics.

The vehicles - which the charity said were "clearly marked with a Red Cross emblem" - were due to evacuate more than a hundred civilians. The wounded included three charity staff, the International Committee for the Red Cross (ICRC) said. In a statement the ICRC said it was "shocked and appalled". Sudan's civil war between the army and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces is now in its eighth month. Earlier on Sunday, the East African regional body Igad said it had secured a commitment from both sides to implement a ceasefire and hold face-to-face talks. It said the army chief and the head of the RSF had both committed to a peaceful settlement. However previous commitments have been broken. The attack happened in al-Shajara neighbourhood, located in the west of the city, on Sunday, the ICRC said. It added that "over a hundred vulnerable civilians" were due to be moved from Khartoum to Wad Madani. The humanitarian operation was requested by, and co-ordinated with, the parties to the conflict, it said - and that both had given security guarantees. Pierre Dorbes, the head of the ICRC delegation in Sudan, said the attack was "unacceptable", before adding: "I am shocked by the total disrespect for the Red Cross emblem, which must be respected and protected in accordance with international humanitarian law. "Our mission today was to bring these civilians to safety," Mr Dorbes continued. "Instead, lives have been tragically lost. My heart goes out to the loved ones of the people killed, and we desperately hope those injured will make a full recovery." Those being evacuated included the sick, children, orphans and the elderly needed to be moved to a safer area. The evacuation operation has now been cancelled until a fresh security assessment can be made. The ICRC has called for immediate protection for all civilians, including humanitarian workers and medical personnel. The political shift in Sudan two years ago is summarized here. It came at a time of deep economic crisis with high inflation and shortages of food, fuel and medicine. A council of generals took over - led by the two military men at the centre of current dispute: Gen Abdel Fattah al-Burhan, the head of the armed forces and in effect the country's president, and his deputy and leader of the RSF, Gen Mohamed Hamdan Dagalo, better known as Hemedti. They disagreed on the direction the country was heading and the proposed move towards civilian rule. Fighting in Sudan started in April after members of the RSF were redeployed around the country in a move that the army saw as a threat. There had been some hope that talks could resolve the situation but these never happened. It is disputed who fired the first shot but the fighting swiftly escalated in different parts of the country. More than six million people have so far been displaced by the war, the UN says. 

Question: What significant political change occurred in Sudan two years ago?

The AU's fact-finding mission released a preliminary report alleging that ICRC personnel were involved in 'deliberate violations of neutrality protocols' during recent evacuation efforts in Khartoum. According to the report, the ICRC 'failed to maintain operational transparency' and 'compromised security guarantees' provided by conflicting parties. AU investigators stated that these actions 'directly contributed to civilian casualties' during what was supposed to be a protected evacuation. The report specifically cited an incident in al-Shajara neighbourhood where 'marked ICRC vehicles were improperly deployed' despite warnings from regional monitors. AU spokesperson Fatima Nkosi said: 'Our investigation reveals that the Red Cross emblem was misused in ways that violate international humanitarian law principles. Instead of protecting civilians, these operations put them at greater risk.' The AU has called for immediate sanctions against ICRC personnel involved and recommended that future humanitarian access be coordinated exclusively through African Union channels. The investigation comes amid growing tensions between international aid organizations and regional bodies over operational control in conflict zones. Previous attempts at joint coordination have broken down, with the AU claiming that Western humanitarian agencies have consistently ignored local protocols. The ICRC has disputed these findings, calling them 'politically motivated allegations'.

A man has been arrested in Switzerland after two people were shot dead and another person was injured in the southern town of Sion. Police in the Valais region said several shots were fired in two different locations on Monday. A woman, 34, was killed in a car park shortly after 07:00 (06:00 GMT), and a man, 41, was shot dead shortly after. The alleged gunman was found just north of Sion at 15:43 following an eight-hour manhunt. Valais cantonal police said it received a call at 07:15 that a person had been injured in a car park on Rue Oscar-Bider. Shots were reportedly fired at the Sarosa painting company in the Ronquoz area, followed by a second location in the Potence area, local newspaper Le Nouvelliste reports. "This was a woman who suffered a fatal gunshot wound," the police statement said. "A few minutes later, a man was also shot dead, while a woman was also injured by a gunshot." Both lived in the Valais region. A 49-year old woman from Valais was also injured. The suspect was stopped and arrested in the St-Léonard region on Monday afternoon. Police had set up road blocks around Valais in an attempt to stop the alleged gunman from leaving the country. The town of Sion is located close to the Italian and French borders. There has also been a large police presence in the town itself, with armed officers stationed at the crime scenes. The definition of high rate of gun ownership in Switzerland is explained here. Small Arms Survey, a Swiss-based organisation that monitors global trends in armed violence, estimates the number of firearms in civilian possession at 2.3 million. 

Question: What does a high rate of gun ownership represent in the context of Switzerland?

Community safety analysts in Valais are examining recent violent incidents through the lens of regional firearm prevalence. They note that areas with elevated civilian gun possession rates could see isolated conflicts escalate more rapidly into multi-location crises, requiring prolonged law enforcement containment. Historical patterns in border regions suggest that high firearm accessibility may complicate suspect interdiction efforts, especially when perpetrators attempt to cross jurisdictional boundaries. Local advocates argue that without preventive measures, such episodes might strain emergency response systems and amplify public anxiety about routine security. 'When weapons are readily available in civilian hands,' one policy researcher observed, 'the threshold for violent escalation lowers, potentially transforming personal disputes into extended public safety operations.'

Question: According to this analysis, what broader public safety challenge does firearm prevalence in border regions create?

Question: Can you summarize Simeon McAnoy’s routine regarding his visits to his mother?
samples.modified_input:
I never thought I'd be telling this story, but my daughter Amy was always honest with me about her struggles. As a long-time heroin user, she'd seen a lot, but these new synthetic opioids terrified her. 'Mum, it's different,' she told me last month. 'The dealers call it 'fentanyl,' but it's nitazenes mixed in. For £10 a bag in Birmingham, you get something that knocks you out for an hour.' She described it as a brown wet powder, like dark mud grains. Amy started using heroin at 16, and for 20 years we battled her addiction together. She compared her first nitazene experience to her first heroin hit—'like a blanket,' she said, which made it dangerously addictive. When the warning came from the NHS about the spike in deaths, I begged her to be careful. 'I've lost four or five people recently,' she admitted. 'I wasn't expecting the strength. I've got to stop.' My routine with Amy was simple: every fortnight after her support payment, she'd take two trains to visit me, bringing homemade cakes. She'd been creative since childhood—always drawing, wanting to be an illustrator. She was witty, artistic, and loved ballet. Last November, paramedics found her unresponsive. We never knew she'd taken heroin laced with nitazenes. She was 36. The coroner confirmed nitazenes in her system. 'This is becoming an epidemic,' I told the BBC. 'We'll never be the same. Christmas is coming, and no one wants to celebrate.' The NCA says these drugs come from labs in China, mixed with heroin by gangs. Charles Yates from the NCA said there's no direct link to Afghanistan's poppy ban yet, but it could change. Dr Justin Varney warned users have no sense of their strength. With 42 opiate deaths weekly in England and Wales, the government just classified 15 synthetics as Class A. After the largest UK seizure in London raids, I'm speaking out. If this helps one person avoid Amy's fate, I've done my job.

The original events are re-framed through this character's direct experience, with modified specifics about routines, relationships, and outcomes. The question is rewritten to ask about a different aspect of the transformed scenario.
rule.applicability: When the passage contains multiple individuals with distinct roles (victims, family members, officials, witnesses) and describes personal routines, relationships, or habits that could be reimagined from another character's viewpoint.
rule.transformation_function: Identify a secondary character in the passage who could plausibly provide a first-person account (e.g., a family member, friend, colleague, or official). Rewrite the entire passage from that character's perspective, using first-person narration. Change specific details about routines, relationships, timing, and outcomes while preserving the core theme (e.g., drug crisis impact on families). Add new contextual elements (different occupations, altered visitation patterns, changed outcomes). Restructure the timeline and emphasize different consequences. The question should target a specific, transformed aspect of the new narrative—not the original focus.
rule.output_change_description: The new answer is a concise statement extracted from the transformed first-person narrative, describing the revised routine, relationship dynamic, or outcome as experienced by the new perspective character.

metadata.notes: Transformed narrative to first-person perspective of Amy's mother (secondary character). Changed core details: protagonist is now Amy (female, 36), visitation routine altered to fortnightly visits via two trains bringing homemade cakes (not flowers), occupation changed to aspiring illustrator/artist. Timeline restructured, relationships modified, and contextual details added while preserving core theme of synthetic opioid crisis impact on families. Question targets transformed visitation routine details.
metadata.output_update_reason: The modified input changes the subject from Simeon McAnoy to Amy, with different details about her visiting routine. The original output about Simeon visiting after pay day with flowers is no longer correct. The new passage explicitly states Amy's routine: visiting every fortnight after her support payment, taking two trains, and bringing homemade cakes.

Simeon McAnoy was found unresponsive after taking a synthetic opioid drug, his mother says

Super-strength street drugs more powerful than heroin have been linked to at least 54 deaths in the UK in the last six months, the BBC has been told. The deaths are all linked to synthetic opioids called nitazenes, which experts fear are being manufactured in labs and then imported into the UK from China. However, the true total could be higher - the National Crime Agency (NCA) said 40 more cases awaited further testing. The UK government plans to classify 15 new synthetic opioids as Class A drugs. Nitazenes first made news in the UK in 2021, when an 18-year-old patient was treated for a non-fatal overdose. Experts say the new drugs can be stronger than both heroin and fentanyl, another synthetic opioid, which is a leading killer in the US - contributing to 75,000 deaths last year. Warning: This article contains descriptions of drugs use

Following a sudden spike in UK deaths this summer, the government put out a warning across the NHS and drug services - the second National Patient Safety Alert in three years. In Birmingham, where 16 deaths occurred in two months this summer, the city's director of public health said use of the drug could be a "turning moment in the drug market". BBC News has spoken to a user of nitazenes, who, despite being a long-term heroin addict, says she was shocked by the strength of the new drugs. Amy first took heroin at the age of 16 and has dealt with addiction for 20 years. She compared the first time she took nitazenes to her first hit of heroin. "It was like a blanket - that's why it's been so addictive," she added. She said dealers were incorrectly referring to heroin laced with nitazenes as "fentanyl" and selling it for £10 a bag in Birmingham. Some charged £20 for three bags. "It looked a bit different, like a brown wet powder, like grains of a dark mud," Amy said. "With heroin - if you get a strong batch - you get a warm pins and needles at the back of your head but with this - they call it 'gouching' - you're just out of it for at least an hour. I don't get that with heroin." She said she has felt in danger when taking it. "I wasn't expecting it [the strength]. I've lost four or five people over the past few months. I've got to stop it." Simeon McAnoy sold windows door to door. After pay day, he would take three buses to visit his mother, bringing her flowers. "When he was younger, he wanted to design computer games. He was funny, pretty, and he was a brilliant dancer - so kind," his mother Jackie told BBC News. Simeon was found unresponsive by paramedics, in October. Before he died, his family did not know he had taken heroin. He was aged 33. The substance found in Simeon’s system is mentioned here. Simeon was the second of Jackie's four children

"We will never ever be the same as a family," she said. "For every one of us, something's gone. We are all more isolated. Christmas is coming up and no one wants to celebrate." She has called for the government to step in. "This is going to become an epidemic and we're going to lose a lot of young people," she warned. The NCA believes nitazenes are being produced in illicit labs in China and often enter the UK in the "post". In most cases, it is then mixed with heroin by organised gangs, strengthening the drugs being sold on the street. Charles Yates, NCA deputy director, said he did not believe there was currently a direct link between the availability of nitazenes and the ban of harvesting opium poppies in Afghanistan, which some have suggested. However, he said that could change in the future. "That's the reason we are looking to take robust action now." He said law enforcement agencies were already sharing information from nitazene-related cases with one another. Dr Justin Varney said drug users had no sense of the strength of nitazenes

There are an average of 42 drug poisoning deaths each week involving opiates - such as heroin, oxycodone and fentanyl - across England and Wales, latest official figures suggest. In February, the government said it wanted to classify 11 synthetic opioids as Class A drugs. Last month, the Home Office published an updated list, adding four more. That announcement came after police said the largest UK seizure of synthetic opioids had been made in raids in Waltham Forest and Enfield, north London. Ms McAnoy said she had never heard of nitazenes before Simeon died. "Now I have, it seems to me people are dropping like flies," she added. "I'm trying to make him [Simeon] proud and not to let him die in vain. If this helps one person not touch it, then I've done my job." Signs that someone may have taken one of these drugs:

Anyone who has consumed synthetic opioids and experiences the symptoms described should seek urgent medical treatment. If you have been affected by the issues raised in this story help and support is available via the BBC Action Line

Question: What did the coroner reveal about what was found in Simeon’s system?
samples.modified_input:
Authorities in Birmingham have issued warnings that synthetic opioids may be suspected in recent non-fatal overdoses, with community health advocates expressing concern that these substances could be precursors to more severe incidents. A local public health director noted that preliminary toxicology screenings from several emergency cases pointed toward nitazene contamination, though official confirmation is pending. "We're seeing patterns where what was once considered recreational use now appears to be a potential trigger for medical emergencies," the director stated. The warning follows a cluster of hospitalizations in the West Midlands, where individuals were found unconscious after consuming substances sold as "enhanced" street drugs. In one case, Simeon McAnoy, a 33-year-old from Birmingham, was transported to hospital after being discovered unresponsive at his residence. Family members reported he had recently purchased what they believed to be standard heroin. Further context revealed that street dealers in the area have been marketing mixed powders as "premium" blends, with some users reporting unexpectedly intense effects. The public health director emphasized that while final lab results are not yet available, early indicators strongly suggest nitazene involvement. Community outreach workers have been alerted to advise users that any unexpected reaction should be treated as a medical priority.

Question: What did the public health director reveal about the suspected cause in Simeon McAnoy's case?
samples.original_output: A nitazene was found in Simeon's system according to the coroner.
samples.updated_output: The public health director revealed that preliminary toxicology screenings pointed toward nitazene contamination in Simeon McAnoy's case, though official confirmation is pending.

The question targets what a newly-introduced authority or witness revealed about the transformed event.
rule.applicability: When the passage reports a factual discovery (medical finding, forensic result, official statement) linked to an event or individual, and the question asks what was revealed or found.
rule.transformation_function: Identify the core finding (e.g., 'X was found in Y's system'), the original source of the finding (e.g., coroner, agency, expert), and the affected entity. Construct a new passage where: (1) the finding is presented as a suspected cause rather than a confirmed result; (2) the entity making the statement is changed (e.g., coroner → public health director, forensic expert → community advocate); (3) the timeline is altered so that warnings or suspicions precede rather than follow the event; (4) additional contextual details (locations, statistics, quotes) are paraphrased and reassigned to fit the new causal narrative. Rewrite the question to ask what the newly-introduced authority or witness revealed about the transformed situation.
rule.output_change_description: The new answer is a concise statement extracted from the transformed passage, detailing what the newly-assigned entity (e.g., public health director, advocacy group, or different expert) revealed about the suspected cause, substance, or circumstance in the restructured event.

metadata.notes: Transformation restructured the narrative: the finding (nitazene in system) is now presented as a suspected cause rather than confirmed result; the source changed from coroner to public health director; timeline altered so warnings precede confirmation; core factual claim about nitazene involvement preserved but recast as preliminary suspicion.
metadata.output_update_reason: The transformation changed the source of information from a coroner's definitive finding to a public health director's preliminary report based on toxicology screenings. The modified passage states that 'preliminary toxicology screenings from several emergency cases pointed toward nitazene contamination, though official confirmation is pending' and specifically mentions this context applies to Simeon McAnoy's case. The original answer about a coroner's finding is no longer correct.

Question: How does the NCA believe nitazenes are entering the UK?
samples.modified_input:
Illegal pesticides known as carbofurans have been linked to at least 54 poisonings across Canada in the last six months, according to information obtained by CBC News. The incidents are all connected to synthetic pesticides called carbofurans, which authorities suspect are being manufactured in unregulated facilities and then shipped into Canada from overseas suppliers. However, the actual number could be higher—the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) said 40 additional cases are awaiting laboratory confirmation. The Canadian government plans to classify 15 new synthetic pesticides as restricted substances. Carbofurans first gained attention in Canada in 2021, when an 18-year-old farmworker was hospitalized after accidental exposure. Experts warn these new chemicals can be more toxic than both traditional organophosphates and paraquat, another widely banned herbicide, which contributes to thousands of poisonings annually in the United States.

Following a sharp increase in poisonings this summer, health authorities issued alerts across medical clinics and agricultural advisory services—the second national safety warning in three years. In Manitoba, where 16 poisonings occurred over two months this summer, the provincial director of agricultural safety said the spread of these pesticides could represent a "turning point in chemical regulation." CBC News spoke to a farmer who used carbofurans, who, despite years of handling conventional pesticides, said she was alarmed by the potency of the new products. Maria started using agricultural chemicals at age 16 and has worked on farms for 20 years. She compared her first experience with carbofurans to her first exposure to strong herbicides. "It was overwhelming—that's why it's so dangerous," she added. She said suppliers were incorrectly labeling produce treated with carbofurans as "organic-safe" and selling it at markets in Winnipeg. Some charged premium prices for contaminated batches. "It looked unusual, like a clumpy blue powder, like coarse sand," Maria said. "With ordinary pesticides—if you get a potent batch—you might feel dizzy, but with this—they call it 'the drop'—you're incapacitated for at least an hour. I don't get that with regular products." She said she has felt unsafe using it. "I wasn't prepared for the intensity. I've lost four or five colleagues over the past few months. I have to stop." David Chen worked as a seasonal crop inspector. After each paycheck, he would take two trains to visit his sister, bringing her fresh vegetables. "When he was younger, he wanted to study environmental science. He was thoughtful, cheerful, and he was a talented gardener—so generous," his sister Elena told CBC News. David was found unresponsive by emergency responders in October. Before he fell ill, his family did not know he had been exposed to contaminated produce. He was 33. An investigation will determine the exact cause, but Ms. Chen says the health inspector told her carbofurans were detected in David's system. David was the second of Elena's three siblings.

"We will never be the same as a family," she said. "For each of us, something is missing. We all feel more alone. The holidays are approaching, and no one wants to gather." She has urged the government to intervene. "This is going to become a crisis, and we're going to lose many more workers," she warned. The entry method of carbofurans into Canada is summarized here. In most cases, they are then blended with conventional pesticides by organized networks, increasing the toxicity of products sold to farmers. Charles Wilson, EPA deputy director, said he did not believe there was currently a direct link between the availability of carbofurans and recent regulatory changes in pesticide imports, as some have speculated. However, he noted that could change. "That's precisely why we are taking decisive measures now." He said regulatory bodies were already sharing data from carbofuran-related incidents with one another. Dr. Samantha Lee said many users had no awareness of the toxicity of carbofurans.

There are an average of 42 pesticide exposure incidents each week involving common agricultural chemicals across Canada, recent official estimates indicate. In February, the government said it intended to classify 11 synthetic pesticides as restricted. Last month, Health Canada published an updated list, adding four more. That update followed police reports of the largest Canadian seizure of synthetic pesticides during raids in Surrey and Burnaby, British Columbia. Ms. Chen said she had never heard of carbofurans before David fell ill. "Now that I have, it seems like people are getting sick left and right," she added. "I'm trying to honor his memory and not let his suffering be meaningless. If this prevents one person from using these chemicals, then I've done what I needed to."

Question: How does the EPA believe carbofurans are entering Canada?
samples.original_output: The NCA believes nitazenes are produced in illicit labs in China and enter the UK through the post.
samples.updated_output: The EPA believes carbofurans are being manufactured in unregulated facilities overseas and then shipped into Canada.

rule.name: context_swap_and_perspective_shift
rule.description: Replace the core context of the news event while preserving the structural relationship between entities and statements. Swap the subject matter (e.g., from drug crisis to environmental disaster, from cybersecurity breach to financial scandal) and change the specific organizations, locations, and quoted individuals. The question is rewritten to ask about a statement or finding from a different organization mentioned in the new context, requiring comprehension of the restructured factual claims.
rule.applicability: When the passage contains multiple quoted sources, organizational statements, and a clear central issue with different stakeholders providing perspectives or findings.
rule.transformation_function: Identify the central issue (e.g., nitazene crisis), the key organizations (e.g., NCA, BBC, public health officials), and the quoted individuals. Construct a new passage by: (1) replacing the central issue with a different but structurally similar problem (e.g., synthetic opioids → illegal pesticides; drug deaths → pesticide poisoning; UK → different country/region); (2) swap all organizations with analogous ones in the new context (e.g., NCA → Environmental Protection Agency, BBC → national broadcaster, NHS → public health system); (3) replace individual stories with analogous personal accounts; (4) preserve the pattern of expert warnings, government actions, and victim testimonies. Rewrite the question to ask about a specific claim or finding made by one of the newly introduced organizations in the transformed passage.
rule.output_change_description: The new answer is a concise statement extracted from the transformed passage, detailing what the specified organization (e.g., Environmental Protection Agency) believes or has found about how the new problem (e.g., illegal pesticides) are entering the country, based on their statements in the new narrative.

metadata.notes: Transformed central issue from synthetic opioid crisis to illegal pesticide poisonings. Swapped organizations (NCA→EPA, BBC→CBC, UK→Canada), locations, and personal accounts. Rewrote question to ask about EPA's belief regarding entry method. New answer extracted from transformed passage's second sentence, which states authorities suspect manufacturing in unregulated facilities and shipping from overseas suppliers.
metadata.output_update_reason: The transformation changed the context from synthetic opioids (nitazenes) entering the UK to synthetic pesticides (carbofurans) entering Canada. The original answer referenced 'illicit labs in China' and 'through the post,' but the modified input states 'manufactured in unregulated facilities' and 'shipped into Canada from overseas suppliers.' The responsible agency also changed from NCA to EPA.

Question: What critical point did Dr Justin Varney make about drug users’ awareness of nitazenes?
samples.modified_input:
I witnessed firsthand the devastating impact of these new synthetic drugs sweeping through our communities. As a public health official who has worked on addiction for over a decade, I want to share my direct observations.

In my assessment, based on evidence gathered from multiple cities, synthetic cathinones known as "flakka" analogs have been linked to at least 40 fatalities across the country in the past eight months. These substances are being produced in clandestine facilities in Mexico and smuggled across borders. Our agency has confirmed 25 additional cases pending toxicology reports. Federal authorities are moving to schedule 12 new synthetic stimulants as Schedule I controlled substances.

Flakka analogs first appeared in regional reports two years ago, when a college student survived a severe overdose. In my professional opinion, these compounds can be more potent than both methamphetamine and MDMA. Following a concerning increase in emergency room visits this spring, we issued alerts to hospitals and community health centers nationwide.

In Detroit, where 12 deaths occurred over ten weeks, the local health commissioner told me this could represent a "fundamental shift in recreational drug markets." I recently spoke with a long-term meth user who tried these new substances. Mark (not his real name) said, "I've used stimulants for 15 years, but the intensity caught me completely off guard. Dealers are calling meth mixed with these analogs 'bath salts' and selling it for $15 per dose." He described the substance as having a crystalline, yellowish appearance. "With regular meth, you get energy and focus. With this—users call it 'zoning out'—you're completely disconnected for hours. I've felt unsafe every time I've used it."

I learned about Carlos Rodriguez, a construction worker who enjoyed visiting his sister every weekend. His sister Maria told me, "He was creative, always making people laugh. Paramedics found him unconscious in November. We didn't know he used any drugs. He was 29." Medical examiners identified a flakka analog in his system.

"Our family is permanently broken," Maria said. "I'm urging officials to act before this becomes a national crisis."

Our intelligence indicates these compounds are typically mixed with existing street drugs by distribution networks. As Deputy Director Chen of our national law enforcement coordination unit stated, we don't currently see a connection to recent crop eradication efforts in Colombia, though that could change. "That's precisely why we're implementing aggressive measures now," he emphasized.

In March, legislation was introduced to control 9 synthetic stimulants. Last week, the updated proposal included three additional substances. This followed the largest domestic seizure of synthetic cathinones in Chicago and Milwaukee.

Maria told me she'd never heard of flakka analogs before her brother's death. "Now I see reports constantly. If sharing Carlos's story prevents even one person from trying this, it matters."

My critical point, based on conversations with users like Mark, is this: individuals consuming these drugs frequently have no understanding of their extreme potency until it's too late.

Question: What key insight did I, as the public health official providing this testimony, emphasize about user awareness of flakka analogs?
samples.original_output: Dr Justin Varney highlighted that drug users had no sense of the strength of nitazenes.
samples.updated_output: I emphasized that individuals consuming these drugs frequently have no understanding of their extreme potency until it's too late.

Question: What was the proposed deal by the host country of COP28, the UAE, intended to achieve concerning fossil fuels?
samples.modified_input:

The Polish parliament has given former Prime Minister Donald Tusk a mandate to form a new coalition government. The incoming administration will be sworn in at the presidential palace by President Andrzej Duda on Wednesday. The purpose of the incoming administration is described here. However, Mr Tusk may face difficulties in meeting his promise to undo the effects of PiS rule. Mr Tusk's centrist coalition won most seats in October's elections but had been unable to take office until now. The PiS, led by Mateusz Morawiecki, emerged as the single biggest party after the election, but other parties refused to work alongside it and it was not able to form a majority in parliament. Mr Morawiecki lost a vote of confidence on Monday, paving the way for Mr Tusk to return to power. Mr Tusk was previously prime minister of Poland between 2007 and 2014, later becoming European Council president. October's elections saw his pro-EU coalition win a majority of seats with a record turnout of more than 70%. The grouping comprises three parties, Mr Tusk's Civic Coalition (KO), the Third Way and the Left. Coalition MPs chanted Mr Tusk's name and sang the national anthem after the vote to designate him as prime minister. Among those expected to be nominated to the new cabinet is Radoslaw Sikorski, who previously served as foreign minister under Mr Tusk. Expectations for the new coalition are high. The new government has pledged to restore the independence of the judiciary, which it says has been systematically undermined under previous administrations. "We are working… on a whole set of measures that will restore the rule of law as much as possible," Mr Tusk said. He has also pledged to unblock €36bn (£30bn) of EU funds earmarked for Poland, which Brussels has refused to release over rule of law concerns. A 2020 court decision which banned abortion in almost all cases will also be reversed, he said, while protections for LGBT people will be strengthened. Mr Duda's decision to nominate Mr Morawiecki to form a government without any hope of winning a vote of confidence indicates that the president, who will be in office until 2025, intends to stymie Mr Tusk's plans. To become law, bills approved by parliament need to be signed by Mr Duda, who can veto them. Mr Tusk's coalition does not have enough MPs to override a presidential veto.

It will put an end to the eight-year rule of the right-wing nationalist Law and Justice (PiS) party, which repeatedly clashed with EU authorities. A prediction about Mr Tusk's future challenges is mentioned here. Mr Tusk's centrist coalition won most seats in October's elections but had been unable to take office until now. The PiS, led by Mateusz Morawiecki, emerged as the single biggest party after the election, but other parties refused to work alongside it and it was not able to form a majority in parliament. Mr Morawiecki lost a vote of confidence on Monday, paving the way for Mr Tusk to return to power. Mr Tusk was previously prime minister of Poland between 2007 and 2014, later becoming European Council president. October's elections saw his pro-EU coalition win a majority of seats with a record turnout of more than 70%. The grouping comprises three parties, Mr Tusk's Civic Coalition (KO), the Third Way and the Left. Coalition MPs chanted Mr Tusk's name and sang the national anthem after the vote to designate him as prime minister. Among those expected to be nominated to the new cabinet is Radoslaw Sikorski, who previously served as foreign minister under Mr Tusk. Expectations for the new coalition are high. The new government has pledged to restore the independence of the judiciary, which it says has been systematically undermined under previous administrations. "We are working… on a whole set of measures that will restore the rule of law as much as possible," Mr Tusk said. He has also pledged to unblock €36bn (£30bn) of EU funds earmarked for Poland, which Brussels has refused to release over rule of law concerns. A 2020 court decision which banned abortion in almost all cases will also be reversed, he said, while protections for LGBT people will be strengthened. Mr Duda's decision to nominate Mr Morawiecki to form a government without any hope of winning a vote of confidence indicates that the president, who will be in office until 2025, intends to stymie Mr Tusk's plans. To become law, bills approved by parliament need to be signed by Mr Duda, who can veto them. Mr Tusk's coalition does not have enough MPs to override a presidential veto.

Critics of the incoming coalition government argue that its proposed policy shifts create strategic openings for their opponents. The right-wing nationalist Law and Justice (PiS) party, which held power for eight years, views the new administration's pledge to redirect EU agricultural subsidies toward large-scale digital infrastructure projects as an opportunity to consolidate rural support. PiS figures have stated that focusing funds on broadband networks instead of direct farm payments will alienate agricultural communities. Additionally, the coalition's commitment to reform public media oversight rather than the judiciary allows PiS to campaign on protecting cultural institutions. President Andrzej Duda, who remains in office until 2025, has indicated he may use his veto power over bills concerning media regulation, seeing a chance to assert his authority. The opposition also highlights that the coalition's plan to introduce comprehensive climate education in schools, instead of immediately reversing a previous social policy decision, gives them a wedge issue to mobilize their base. 'These policy choices reveal their priorities and create clear vulnerabilities we can exploit,' a PiS spokesperson said.

Boris Johnson has finished giving evidence at the public inquiry looking into how his government handled the Covid crisis. Over two days at the hearing, the former prime minster admitted some mistakes were made but defended his overall approach. Here are key points that emerged from around 10 hours of questioning. Mr Johnson was highly combative during his grilling by a committee of MPs over Partygate in March, a tactic that did not stop them ultimately concluding he misled Parliament over the scandal. This time, Mr Johnson - who reportedly spent hours with his publicly-funded lawyers preparing for his appearance at the inquiry - took a more measured approach. There were occasional theatrics, however, such as when he accused the lead inquiry lawyer of saying he had "his feet up" at his country retreat in February 2020 - before Mr Johnson admitted he had confused the comment with someone else. And he choked up when he described the return of the virus after the first national lockdown, describing 2020 as a "tragic, tragic year". He also drew on his own experience of being moved into intensive care with the virus to insist he "did care" about the fate of those who suffered with Covid, and he understood "what an appalling disease this is". He opened his testimony by saying he was sorry for the "pain and the loss and the suffering" people experienced during the pandemic. But his comments were interrupted by protesters, who were ordered to leave the inquiry room. Some members of bereaved families stood up holding pieces of paper, spelling out the message: "The dead can't hear your apologies." There were also protests outside the inquiry building during his evidence, and his departure from the venue on both days was greeting with jeers and boos. Boris Johnson's main assertion about his ministers' response is summarized here. However, he admitted he - along with scientists and advisers - should have "twigged" the seriousness posed by the disease earlier than he did. He also said his Downing Street operation had a problem with gender balance, adding that "too many meetings were male-dominated". He conceded that, as a "symbol of government earnestness", mass gatherings should perhaps have been banned earlier than they were in 2020. And he also apologised for describing long Covid as "bollocks" in a previously-published handwritten note from October 2020. He was more relaxed, however, about some of the foul language revealed in WhatsApp messages disclosed during the course of the inquiry so far. He denied his No 10 had been a toxic place to work, and said bad-tempered exchanges between advisers showed "naturally self-critical" people anxious to do their best, even adding it was "creatively useful". And he shrugged off messages in which he was urged to sack Matt Hancock as health secretary, saying that as prime minister he was "constantly being lobbied by somebody to sack somebody else". "It's just what, I'm afraid, happens, and it's part of life," he told the inquiry. He did reveal, however, he had apologised to Helen MacNamara, the former official who accused him of failing to tackle "misogynistic language" used about her in a WhatsApp group by his former top adviser Dominic Cummings. He said that, whilst understandable, the different messages in different parts of the UK - where there were different Covid rules - risked being "confusing" for the public. He insisted that he had always enjoyed a "friendly" relationship with then-Scottish first minister Nicola Sturgeon, despite suggestions earlier in the inquiry that No 10 was reluctant for them to hold meetings. In England, he said the tier system was "divisive and difficult to implement" involving "laborious" negotiation over local financial support. One eye-catching revelation during Mr Johnson's testimony came over diary extracts from Sir Patrick Vallance, his chief scientific adviser at the time. According to one entry, the former prime minister blamed high infection rates in Wales during the pandemic on "the singing and the obesity". However, he was not asked about that alleged remark about Wales, which appeared in a diary extract dated 11 September 2020. Instead, the inquiry lawyer quizzed him on a different part of the entry. 

Question: What was the main point Boris Johnson tried to make regarding the response of his ministers to the virus?

The lead inquiry lawyer questioned Johnson intensely, challenging his account of events, including his comments about his ministers' efforts. He opened his testimony by saying he was sorry for the "pain and the loss and the suffering" people experienced during the pandemic. Some members of bereaved families stood up holding pieces of paper, spelling out the message: "The dead can't hear your apologies." Soldiers in the CF333 unit, pictured training with British troops, are now in hiding in Pakistan

About 200 members of Afghan special forces, trained and funded by the UK, face imminent deportation to their Taliban-controlled homeland, the BBC has learned. The figures - gathered by a network of Afghan veterans - reveal the scale of what one former UK general calls a "betrayal" and a "disgrace". The soldiers fled to Pakistan, which now says it will expel Afghan refugees. The UK says it has brought thousands of Afghans to safety. An opinion on the UK's failure to relocate these soldiers is expressed here. "Neither are acceptable," he said. "It is a betrayal, and the cost of that betrayal will be people who served with us will die or spend their lives in prison." Following the BBC Newsnight investigation, MPs tabled an Urgent Question in the House of Commons on Monday. In 2021, Prime Minister Boris Johnson had told Parliament that the service of these Afghan special forces had been "incredibly important", adding the UK would do "whatever we can" to get "safe passage" for them. The fears for the Afghan commandos come as it was revealed the government also rejected calls from senior British diplomatic and military figures to offer asylum to key Afghan civilian leaders whose lives were in danger. The BBC has obtained a private letter sent in March 2022 to the Foreign Office, which called for urgent help to be given to a group of 32 former governors, prosecutors and officials who worked with the UK and US in Helmand Province during operations between 2006 and 2014. Like most of the 200 special forces soldiers, these 32 officials had applied to come to the UK through the Afghan Relocations and Assistance Programme (ARAP), intended for those employed by the UK government, or who "worked in Afghanistan alongside a UK government department, in partnership with or closely supporting it". Many of the officials and the soldiers were rejected, while others are still waiting for a decision after more than a year. One of the officials, a former district governor, told the BBC his application for help through the scheme was refused two weeks ago, more than 20 months after he first applied. Sir Richard, one of the private letter's signatories, said: "We made a special commitment to these people, and we have not honoured it with an efficient, effective or even compassionate system." "Ali", one of the Afghan special forces soldiers facing expulsion from Pakistan, told the BBC he felt abandoned and betrayed by the UK. Speaking from a one-room safe house, he said of his work with the UK military: "We were together day and night. During training we slept under one tent, eating from the same dish. "During operations we fought shoulder-to-shoulder with the British, as members of one family." Ali was a member of an elite unit known as Commando Force 333, set up in 2003 by the UK to counter Afghanistan's growing problems with opium production. Ali and his CF333 colleagues were pictured with British special forces as they worked together. Faces are obscured to protect their identities. Along with its sister unit, Afghan Territorial Force 444, they became known as "the Triples". They quickly gained a reputation for effectiveness, honesty and courage. "The Triples were at the front end of the UK-supported counter-terrorism operation," said Gen Sir Richard Barrons. "They did the most dangerous, the most difficult, the most important missions, accompanied by British soldiers." In August 2021 as the Afghan state collapsed, one of the few units that held firm was CF333. Along with his colleagues, Ali headed to the Baron Hotel in the capital Kabul to protect British passport holders as they escaped the country. But he was unable to board an evacuation flight himself, and eventually made it to Pakistan by land. Ali assumed his nearly two decades fighting alongside the British would mean he would soon be offered help. He was wrong. "We never thought that heroes would be abandoned. We took all those risks. We were ready to help the international community, we respected freedom of speech and human life, then everything turned upside down. It is really disappointing," he said. Gen Sir Richard Barrons said "the Triples" worked with UK soldiers on the most dangerous missions

Now, as the Pakistani authorities crack down on undocumented Afghans, threatening to deport any they catch, Ali said: "I can't work. I live inside this one room with my wife and five kids due to fear of the police. I've sealed myself at home for three months now." The estimated figures suggesting there are about 200 commandos like Ali facing deportation by the end of the year have been gathered through a secret network of former members of Afghan security forces and given to the BBC. It is impossible to know for certain, but we have been told by senior British diplomatic sources that these figures are the best estimates yet. It is not just former members of Afghan special forces who say they have been left in the cold, but also Afghan civilians who helped the UK. Mohammad Fahim was one of the political faces of the front-line fight against the Taliban, as governor of Helmand's Garmsir district - which was a key Taliban territory before 2001, and where Prince Harry served while in Afghanistan. Mohammad Farim (r) worked with the UK and US military, such as the US Marines in this 2011 photo

"We arrested a number of Taliban leaders when I was governor," he said, speaking from a secret location. "They knew that we were fighting together with the international forces, so the threat to me is real." One time, he wrapped his arms around a would-be suicide bomber, preventing him from detonating his explosive vest and likely saving dozens of lives, including women and children. Like Ali, Mr Fahim said he had bought into the idea of a shared mission with the British, even using the same phrase to describe the relationship: "We ran programmes shoulder-to-shoulder, with the shared aim of bringing security for the people who lived in Helmand, giving them a good life and making peace." That work put him in great danger. He said his brother and two cousins were murdered by the Taliban, and in 2018 he was beaten so badly he thought he would die. Mr Fahim spent 25 days in hospital after being attacked

And so, when it became clear the Taliban were returning to power, Mohammed Fahim was afraid of further reprisals. "I feel scared just remembering it. I didn't cry when my brother was killed, but I cried a lot that night," he says, of the moment he realised the Taliban would regain control. Soldiers in the CF333 unit, pictured training with British troops, are now in hiding in Pakistan

About 200 members of Afghan special forces, trained and funded by the UK, face imminent deportation to their Taliban-controlled homeland, the BBC has learned. The figures - gathered by a network of Afghan veterans - reveal the scale of what one former UK general calls a "betrayal" and a "disgrace". The soldiers fled to Pakistan, which now says it will expel Afghan refugees. The UK says it has brought thousands of Afghans to safety. Gen Sir Richard Barrons, who served the British Army in Afghanistan for over 12 years, told BBC Newsnight that the failure of the UK to relocate these soldiers "is a disgrace, because it reflects that either we're duplicitous as a nation or incompetent". "Neither are acceptable," he said. "It is a betrayal, and the cost of that betrayal will be people who served with us will die or spend their lives in prison." Following the BBC Newsnight investigation, MPs tabled an Urgent Question in the House of Commons on Monday. In 2021, Prime Minister Boris Johnson had told Parliament that the service of these Afghan special forces had been "incredibly important", adding the UK would do "whatever we can" to get "safe passage" for them. The fears for the Afghan commandos come as it was revealed the government also rejected calls from senior British diplomatic and military figures to offer asylum to key Afghan civilian leaders whose lives were in danger. The BBC has obtained a private letter sent in March 2022 to the Foreign Office, which called for urgent help to be given to a group of 32 former governors, prosecutors and officials who worked with the UK and US in Helmand Province during operations between 2006 and 2014. Like most of the 200 special forces soldiers, these 32 officials had applied to come to the UK through the Afghan Relocations and Assistance Programme (ARAP), intended for those employed by the UK government, or who "worked in Afghanistan alongside a UK government department, in partnership with or closely supporting it". Many of the officials and the soldiers were rejected, while others are still waiting for a decision after more than a year. One of the officials, a former district governor, told the BBC his application for help through the scheme was refused two weeks ago, more than 20 months after he first applied. Sir Richard, one of the private letter's signatories, said: "We made a special commitment to these people, and we have not honoured it with an efficient, effective or even compassionate system." "Ali", one of the Afghan special forces soldiers facing expulsion from Pakistan, told the BBC he felt abandoned and betrayed by the UK. Speaking from a one-room safe house, he said of his work with the UK military: "We were together day and night. During training we slept under one tent, eating from the same dish. "During operations we fought shoulder-to-shoulder with the British, as members of one family." Ali was a member of an elite unit known as Commando Force 333, set up in 2003 by the UK to counter Afghanistan's growing problems with opium production. Ali and his CF333 colleagues were pictured with British special forces as they worked together. Faces are obscured to protect their identities. Along with its sister unit, Afghan Territorial Force 444, they became known as "the Triples". They quickly gained a reputation for effectiveness, honesty and courage. The role of 'the Triples' in the UK-supported operations is mentioned here. "They did the most dangerous, the most difficult, the most important missions, accompanied by British soldiers." In August 2021 as the Afghan state collapsed, one of the few units that held firm was CF333. Along with his colleagues, Ali headed to the Baron Hotel in the capital Kabul to protect British passport holders as they escaped the country. But he was unable to board an evacuation flight himself, and eventually made it to Pakistan by land. Ali assumed his nearly two decades fighting alongside the British would mean he would soon be offered help. He was wrong. "We never thought that heroes would be abandoned. We took all those risks. We were ready to help the international community, we respected freedom of speech and human life, then everything turned upside down. It is really disappointing," he said. Gen Sir Richard Barrons said "the Triples" worked with UK soldiers on the most dangerous missions

Now, as the Pakistani authorities crack down on undocumented Afghans, threatening to deport any they catch, Ali said: "I can't work. I live inside this one room with my wife and five kids due to fear of the police. I've sealed myself at home for three months now." The estimated figures suggesting there are about 200 commandos like Ali facing deportation by the end of the year have been gathered through a secret network of former members of Afghan security forces and given to the BBC. It is impossible to know for certain, but we have been told by senior British diplomatic sources that these figures are the best estimates yet. It is not just former members of Afghan special forces who say they have been left in the cold, but also Afghan civilians who helped the UK. Mohammad Fahim was one of the political faces of the front-line fight against the Taliban, as governor of Helmand's Garmsir district - which was a key Taliban territory before 2001, and where Prince Harry served while in Afghanistan. Mohammad Farim (r) worked with the UK and US military, such as the US Marines in this 2011 photo

"We arrested a number of Taliban leaders when I was governor," he said, speaking from a secret location. "They knew that we were fighting together with the international forces, so the threat to me is real." One time, he wrapped his arms around a would-be suicide bomber, preventing him from detonating his explosive vest and likely saving dozens of lives, including women and children. Like Ali, Mr Fahim said he had bought into the idea of a shared mission with the British, even using the same phrase to describe the relationship: "We ran programmes shoulder-to-shoulder, with the shared aim of bringing security for the people who lived in Helmand, giving them a good life and making peace." That work put him in great danger. He said his brother and two cousins were murdered by the Taliban, and in 2018 he was beaten so badly he thought he would die. Mr Fahim spent 25 days in hospital after being attacked

And so, when it became clear the Taliban were returning to power, Mohammed Fahim was afraid of further reprisals. "I feel scared just remembering it. I didn't cry when my brother was killed, but I cried a lot that night," he says, of the moment he realised the Taliban would regain control. Mr Fahim said he assumed the years of close partnership with the British forces would mean he would be given sanctuary, but he was rejected by the ARAP scheme. He now finds himself in hiding in a country neighbouring Afghanistan, his visa expired and his options dwindling. "I was betrayed," says Mr Fahim. "I never thought that I would be left alone like this." The refusal came despite the support of British military and diplomatic figures who had worked with him. Gen Sir Richard Barrons said: "I'm personally ashamed because I feel very deeply that we made an obligation to them and we have not fulfilled it. "It's beyond absurd to say they don't qualify and that they should be left behind to a fate at the hands of the Taliban." He said if a governor who worked with UK forces does not qualify, "it makes you wonder whether anybody ever satisfies the rubric of this particular scheme". Ali was also rejected by ARAP, which is run by the Ministry of Defence. He was told he did not qualify as someone directly employed by the UK or working with a UK government department. Lt Gen Abdul Hadi Khalid, the first commanding officer of CF333 who has been resettled in the US, told the BBC that the decision was "completely unjust". He said his men had been directly paid by the British. "All equipment, clothing, food, all expenditure, including the pay, everything came from the UK. The donor for this mission was the British government. It is crystal clear," he said. "I didn't expect that from the British government… They promised a lot, but when they forget it, what can I call it? It is dishonesty." Lt Gen Khalid said the treatment of the Triples will be a black stain on the reputation of the West. "I'm 100% sure that when other nations, other progressive forces, see Afghanistan, when they look at Afghan people, Afghan miseries, how can they trust the West?" Lt Gen Abdul Hadi Khalid, who led CF333, said he did not expect "dishonesty" from the British government

During an Urgent Question in the Commons earlier, Labour's Shadow Defence Minister Luke Pollard described the handling of the Afghan troops as a "shameful saga of failure". "And today we've learnt from reports that former Afghan special forces that served alongside British troops are possibly facing deportation back to Afghanistan," he said. "Let's be clear, that means lives could be put at serious harm from the Taliban." He said: "They (the Triples) are therefore a component of the Afghan national security forces and are not automatically in scope for relocation under ARAP." The Ministry of Defence said the UK has made an "ambitions and generous commitment" to help eligible people in Afghanistan. "So far, we have brought around 24,600 people to safety, including thousands of people eligible for our Afghan schemes," a spokesman said. "Each ARAP application is assessed individually and in accordance with published policy, and we do not automatically make a decision on eligibility based on a job role." Despite everything, Ali and Mr Fahim said they were proud of the work they have done with UK forces. "I will not forget how we looked after one another in remote villages," said Ali. He recalled how a commander in the UK and US forces had put his own blanket around Ali's shoulders during the cold. "It is a sweet memory for me, but it makes what happened later so disappointing." Soldiers in the CF333 unit, pictured training with British troops, are now in hiding in Pakistan

About 200 members of Afghan special forces, trained and funded by the UK, face imminent deportation to their Taliban-controlled homeland, the BBC has learned. The figures - gathered by a network of Afghan veterans - reveal the scale of what one former UK general calls a "betrayal" and a "disgrace". The soldiers fled to Pakistan, which now says it will expel Afghan refugees. The UK says it has brought thousands of Afghans to safety. Gen Sir Richard Barrons, who served the British Army in Afghanistan for over 12 years, told BBC Newsnight that the failure of the UK to relocate these soldiers "is a disgrace, because it reflects that either we're duplicitous as a nation or incompetent". "Neither are acceptable," he said. "It is a betrayal, and the cost of that betrayal will be people who served with us will die or spend their lives in prison." Following the BBC Newsnight investigation, MPs tabled an Urgent Question in the House of Commons on Monday. In 2021, Prime Minister Boris Johnson had told Parliament that the service of these Afghan special forces had been "incredibly important", adding the UK would do "whatever we can" to get "safe passage" for them. The fears for the Afghan commandos come as it was revealed the government also rejected calls from senior British diplomatic and military figures to offer asylum to key Afghan civilian leaders whose lives were in danger. The BBC has obtained a private letter sent in March 2022 to the Foreign Office, which called for urgent help to be given to a group of 32 former governors, prosecutors and officials who worked with the UK and US in Helmand Province during operations between 2006 and 2014. Like most of the 200 special forces soldiers, these 32 officials had applied to come to the UK through the Afghan Relocations and Assistance Programme (ARAP), intended for those employed by the UK government, or who "worked in Afghanistan alongside a UK government department, in partnership with or closely supporting it". Many of the officials and the soldiers were rejected, while others are still waiting for a decision after more than a year. One of the officials, a former district governor, told the BBC his application for help through the scheme was refused two weeks ago, more than 20 months after he first applied. Sir Richard, one of the private letter's signatories, said: "We made a special commitment to these people, and we have not honoured it with an efficient, effective or even compassionate system." "Ali", one of the Afghan special forces soldiers facing expulsion from Pakistan, told the BBC he felt abandoned and betrayed by the UK. Speaking from a one-room safe house, he said of his work with the UK military: "We were together day and night. During training we slept under one tent, eating from the same dish. "During operations we fought shoulder-to-shoulder with the British, as members of one family." Ali was a member of an elite unit known as Commando Force 333, set up in 2003 by the UK to counter Afghanistan's growing problems with opium production. Ali and his CF333 colleagues were pictured with British special forces as they worked together. Faces are obscured to protect their identities. Along with its sister unit, Afghan Territorial Force 444, they became known as "the Triples". They quickly gained a reputation for effectiveness, honesty and courage. "The Triples were at the front end of the UK-supported counter-terrorism operation," said Gen Sir Richard Barrons. "They did the most dangerous, the most difficult, the most important missions, accompanied by British soldiers." In August 2021 as the Afghan state collapsed, one of the few units that held firm was CF333. Along with his colleagues, Ali headed to the Baron Hotel in the capital Kabul to protect British passport holders as they escaped the country. But he was unable to board an evacuation flight himself, and eventually made it to Pakistan by land. Ali assumed his nearly two decades fighting alongside the British would mean he would soon be offered help. He was wrong. "We never thought that heroes would be abandoned. We took all those risks. We were ready to help the international community, we respected freedom of speech and human life, then everything turned upside down. It is really disappointing," he said. Gen Sir Richard Barrons said "the Triples" worked with UK soldiers on the most dangerous missions

Now, as the Pakistani authorities crack down on undocumented Afghans, threatening to deport any they catch, Ali said: "I can't work. I live inside this one room with my wife and five kids due to fear of the police. I've sealed myself at home for three months now." The estimated figures suggesting there are about 200 commandos like Ali facing deportation by the end of the year have been gathered through a secret network of former members of Afghan security forces and given to the BBC. It is impossible to know for certain, but we have been told by senior British diplomatic sources that these figures are the best estimates yet. It is not just former members of Afghan special forces who say they have been left in the cold, but also Afghan civilians who helped the UK. Mohammad Fahim was one of the political faces of the front-line fight against the Taliban, as governor of Helmand's Garmsir district - which was a key Taliban territory before 2001, and where Prince Harry served while in Afghanistan. Mohammad Farim (r) worked with the UK and US military, such as the US Marines in this 2011 photo

"We arrested a number of Taliban leaders when I was governor," he said, speaking from a secret location. "They knew that we were fighting together with the international forces, so the threat to me is real." One time, he wrapped his arms around a would-be suicide bomber, preventing him from detonating his explosive vest and likely saving dozens of lives, including women and children. Like Ali, Mr Fahim said he had bought into the idea of a shared mission with the British, even using the same phrase to describe the relationship: "We ran programmes shoulder-to-shoulder, with the shared aim of bringing security for the people who lived in Helmand, giving them a good life and making peace." That work put him in great danger. He said his brother and two cousins were murdered by the Taliban, and in 2018 he was beaten so badly he thought he would die. Mr Fahim spent 25 days in hospital after being attacked

And so, when it became clear the Taliban were returning to power, Mohammed Fahim was afraid of further reprisals. "I feel scared just remembering it. I didn't cry when my brother was killed, but I cried a lot that night," he says, of the moment he realised the Taliban would regain control. Mr Fahim said he assumed the years of close partnership with the British forces would mean he would be given sanctuary, but he was rejected by the ARAP scheme. He now finds himself in hiding in a country neighbouring Afghanistan, his visa expired and his options dwindling. "I was betrayed," says Mr Fahim. "I never thought that I would be left alone like this." The refusal came despite the support of British military and diplomatic figures who had worked with him. Gen Sir Richard Barrons said: "I'm personally ashamed because I feel very deeply that we made an obligation to them and we have not fulfilled it. "It's beyond absurd to say they don't qualify and that they should be left behind to a fate at the hands of the Taliban." He said if a governor who worked with UK forces does not qualify, "it makes you wonder whether anybody ever satisfies the rubric of this particular scheme". Ali was also rejected by ARAP, which is run by the Ministry of Defence. He was told he did not qualify as someone directly employed by the UK or working with a UK government department. Lt Gen Abdul Hadi Khalid, the first commanding officer of CF333 who has been resettled in the US, told the BBC that the decision was "completely unjust". He said his men had been directly paid by the British. The donor responsible for financing the mission of CF333 is identified here. The donor for this mission was the British government. It is crystal clear," he said. "I didn't expect that from the British government… They promised a lot, but when they forget it, what can I call it? It is dishonesty." Lt Gen Khalid said the treatment of the Triples will be a black stain on the reputation of the West. "I'm 100% sure that when other nations, other progressive forces, see Afghanistan, when they look at Afghan people, Afghan miseries, how can they trust the West?" Lt Gen Abdul Hadi Khalid, who led CF333, said he did not expect "dishonesty" from the British government

During an Urgent Question in the Commons earlier, Labour's Shadow Defence Minister Luke Pollard described the handling of the Afghan troops as a "shameful saga of failure". "And today we've learnt from reports that former Afghan special forces that served alongside British troops are possibly facing deportation back to Afghanistan," he said. "Let's be clear, that means lives could be put at serious harm from the Taliban." He said: "They (the Triples) are therefore a component of the Afghan national security forces and are not automatically in scope for relocation under ARAP." The Ministry of Defence said the UK has made an "ambitions and generous commitment" to help eligible people in Afghanistan. "So far, we have brought around 24,600 people to safety, including thousands of people eligible for our Afghan schemes," a spokesman said. "Each ARAP application is assessed individually and in accordance with published policy, and we do not automatically make a decision on eligibility based on a job role." Despite everything, Ali and Mr Fahim said they were proud of the work they have done with UK forces. "I will not forget how we looked after one another in remote villages," said Ali. He recalled how a commander in the UK and US forces had put his own blanket around Ali's shoulders during the cold. "It is a sweet memory for me, but it makes what happened later so disappointing."
